Senses.Explanation: One stroke of a blade leaves two separate pieces: the image is a single completed cut rather than repeated or partial cutting. Ying'an Tanhua and Longtan Zhiyuan make that compact result a short public answer; Dahui Zonggao makes it a direct command in daily activity; Fenyang Shanzhao calls for a 'one-cut-two-pieces person'; and Changqing Huileng checks the formula by saying that even one cut into two pieces does not yet qualify someone as a lineage teacher. These named answer, command, person-label, and critical uses establish a reusable formula and the Chan bend while leaving the figurative object unspecified.

Senses.Explanation: “Everything is already complete” appears as a Fayan-house characterization, a direct interview answer, and an exhortation to take up what requires no added construction. Literally, everything is already complete or ready-made . The phrase enters the Chan record in Dizang's answer to Fayan: when discussing the buddha teaching, everything is already complete. Later records quote that exchange and list “everything is already complete” as the characteristic wording of the Fayan house. It also appears as an answer to “What is the Fayan house?” and in Dahui's instruction to step back, look for oneself, and directly take responsibility for what is already complete. The record does not treat the formula as a licence for mere repetition: Lushan Tianran asks whether saying it would mean an entire summer had passed in vain, while another exchange answers a student's repetition with blows and “Do not cite this wrongly to people.” The Chan deviation is therefore a house formula, answer, and contested quotation attached to the Dizang–Fayan encounter, not merely the ordinary statement that supplies are ready.

AlternateTargets: draw all the West River's water into one mouthful

Mazu and Pang Yun West River case
when you drink up the West River I will tell you
Senses.Explanation: An impossible-scale condition in Mazu Daoyi's answer to Pang Yun: Pang asks, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' and Mazu replies, 'When you drink up all the West River's water in one mouthful, I will tell you.' The exact line occurs 329 times in 139 allowlisted texts. Later records preserve that condition as a named case line, quote it, turn it into a fresh question, answer it, and build new physical challenges from it. Baiyun Shouduan says that after the one-mouthful drink no drop remains through all antiquity, then calls Mazu's mouth regrettably narrow. An unnamed music-bureau officer sets the West River line aside and asks Yunding Defu to swallow the dismounting platform; Yunding spreads both hands and requests that it be brought. An unnamed monk asks Yuanwu Keqin what about drinking the river, and Yuanwu answers, 'The bright sun adorns the sky.' Wuzu Fayan repeats the line to his assembly and extends it to reaching the bottom of a ten-thousand-fathom pool. Wuchu Daguan quotes Mazu and supplies a different answer to Pang's question, waiting for empty space to fall. These are attested continuations of one Mazu line; the entry does not turn the impossible act into an unstated universal meaning.
Senses.Note: The exact line has 329 matches in 139 files; the shorter opening 'in one mouthful drink up all' has 398 matches in 153. Mazu's full conditional 'when you drink up all the West River's water in one mouthful' occurs 151 times in 95 files. No required definition formula occurs. The preserved witnesses include the founding exchange, verse commentary, Baiyun's new test modeled on the line, Yuanwu's direct answer, Wuzu's address extending the river image to the bottom of a deep pool, and Wuchu's replacement answer. The phrase remains a line spoken in a named public case and a subject of later public questioning.

Senses.Explanation: The one-word barrier is the monastic name for Yunmen’s recurrent single-graph answers, established by an explicit corpus naming formula. The Human and Celestial Eyes supplies the corpus's naming formula: after examples of Yunmen answering prompts with a single graph—‘ancestor’ to ‘what is Yunmen's sword?,’ ‘mound’ to ‘what is within the mysterious?,’ ‘bones’ or ‘a corpse’ to ‘what is the hair-blown sword?,’ and ‘everywhere’ to ‘what is the eye of the true teaching?’—it says that Yunmen often responded to encounters this way, ‘therefore the monasteries named it the one-word barrier.’ Later texts consequently pair ‘Yunmen's one-word barrier’ with Linji's three mysteries, Caoshan's three falls, and other house-associated rosters. A later verse repeats ‘one-word barrier’ and asks why it remains single rather than becoming a pair. The term names the rostered one-word response, not every ordinary barrier containing one written character.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes one-finger Chan in these Chan records. Its wording is "one-finger Chan." The phrase names Juzhi's recorded use of a raised finger in public interviews. A later record states the visible rule directly: "Whenever someone came, Master Juzhi only extended one finger; he called it one-finger Chan" (俱胝和尚逢人但伸一指頭，喚做一指頭禪). In the transmitted case, Tianlong raises one finger to Juzhi; afterward, whenever students ask, Juzhi raises one finger, and before dying he says, "I obtained Tianlong's one-finger Chan; through my whole life I could not use it up" (吾得天龍一指頭禪，一生用不盡). The record also preserves criticism rather than making the label an unquestioned formula: Xuansha says he would have broken the finger, Caoshan faults Juzhi's taking it up, and Sanshan asks, "What connection does one-finger Chan have? It cheated that monk and buried him alive his whole life" (一指頭禪有甚交涉？賺殺阿僧終身活埋). Its Chan-specific bend is thus a named, publicly repeated response inherited from Tianlong and continually examined by later masters.

Senses.Explanation: “A day without work is a day without food” is preserved as Baizhang’s saying, repeated as a communal rule, and versified as the house style of working for food. Literally, “one day not working, one day not eating.” The Chan institutional record attributes the saying to Baizhang and ties it to shared manual labor: the monastic regulations say that even in old age he “shared the community's labor” and regularly said the line. The same regulations later call it “the warning of the ancients” when directing the community to attend communal work. Xutang's record adds that at age ninety-five Baizhang's hoe, cutting tool, rain cape, and bamboo hat never left him. Hongzhi quotes the saying and calls “farming to obtain food to eat” “the house style” . Its Zen deviation is institutional and explicit: a maxim attached to Baizhang becomes the recorded house rule for Baizhang’s and the community’s agricultural labor.

Senses.Explanation: One blind person leading many blind people is an unseeing guide drawing followers into the same danger. Yulin Tongxiu, Miyun Yuanwu, Dufeng Benshan, and Daxiu Zhu all complete the image with the blind group being led into a fire pit. Tian'an Sheng and Shunde use the same line while appraising inherited cases, so the phrase is a verdict on transmission without seeing.

Senses.Explanation: “Not wearing a single thread” names complete nakedness and is extended to a person from whom nothing further can be stripped or removed. Literally, “not hanging a single thread”: not wearing even one strand of clothing. The late Chan records deploy nakedness as a description of a person after successive stripping: Xueguan compares it to taking off clothes and undoing a belt, layer after layer, then asks what could still be removed from “a fellow not wearing a single thread” . Other records pair the phrase with “coming and going freely” or with “the myriad forms all manifest” . The Zen bend is therefore directly visible in its use as an appraisal of a person rather than only a state of undress. The records do not define an inner state behind the image, and this entry does not supply one.

Senses.Explanation: A single blade of grass is lifted, used, or contrasted with a great body and the whole earth in recurring public statements. The Chan corpus loads this smallest ordinary object through a set of reversible public formulas. Most prominently, Mi'an Xianjie may 'take a single blade of grass and make it a sixteen-foot golden body, and take the sixteen-foot golden body and make it a single blade of grass.' The same blade can found a monastery or display jeweled halls and jade palaces. Baiyun Duan's saying makes the relation reversible: after one true sweat, jeweled halls appear atop a blade of grass; without it, even jeweled halls are covered by the blade. Dahui accepts the first clause but warns that the second may deceive the hearer. A separate inherited encounter supplies another deployment: Sudhana picks a blade of grass from the ground as the medicine requested by Manjusri, who says that this medicine can kill and can give life. The Chan-specific bend lies in how the records repeatedly place the concrete blade in reversible comparison with a buddha-body, a monastery, palaces, and medicine, while later masters quote, test, and qualify those formulas.

Senses.Explanation: A single move, play, or stroke is one deliberate action within an encounter. Chan speakers use the counting phrase for getting a move in first, reserving a final move, missing one move, or demanding the move that changes the situation. The game-like noun appears in recurring Chan compounds: "let one move pass" (放過一著, 617 occurrences), "the final move" (末後一著, 104), "the upward move" (向上一著, 279), "one move ahead" (先一著, 38), and the suffixed "one move" (一著子, 601). A case-comment collection appraises an earlier response as "precisely letting one move pass," then adds "danger" (正是放過一著；險). A lamp address pairs "Linji's vanguard—let one move pass" with "Deshan's later command—set it aside" (臨濟先鋒，放過一著；德山後令，且在一邊). Questions ask, "before living beings and buddhas arose, where did one move fall?" (生佛未興時，一著落在甚麼處). Feiyin says, "present one move face to face; the person concerned must personally take it up" (覿面提持個一著，當人要在親領略). These uses support the ordinary move/play sense while showing its Chan deployment as question, appraisal, sequence, and named move.

Senses.Explanation: Huineng defines single conduct in every activity as carrying a straightforward mind without attachment through walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, and rejects motionless sitting as its definition. Huineng uses “single conduct in every activity” for carrying one straightforward mind without attachment through walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. His Platform Record explicitly rejects immobile sitting and suppression of thoughts as the meaning: that account would make it like insentient things and an obstruction to the Way. Huineng first defines it as “at all times, while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, constantly carry a straightforward mind” , and then as carrying a straightforward mind “without attachment to anything” . The Patriarchal Hall Collection preserves the parallel definition: “in every place, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, all is one straightforward mind; this is the site of the Way, this is the pure land” . Huineng's rejected account says that sitting without moving and suppressing thoughts is “single conduct in every activity”; he answers that this is “the same as insentient things” and “a condition obstructing the Way” . Qisong's praise of another Platform edition gives a distinct formulation within the same named compound: “the single aspect of the realm of things” , under which “although the many good acts differ, all are made correct in a single conduct” .

Senses.Explanation: 一轉語 is a word that turns an encounter at the point where its inherited answer, question, or impasse can no longer simply be repeated. In the wild-fox case, an old man asks Baizhang Huaihai to supply one; Baizhang’s 不昧因果 changes the answer on which the whole case turns. The parallel records repeat that same case family and are not seven independent inventions of the phrase. Tianyi Huai asks for a turning word on behalf of the Buddha when the demon king’s vow leaves the usual contrast of Buddha and demon unusable; later commentators test proposed replies rather than treating the label as praise by itself. Xiangcheng Shun says Sheng’s single turning word won him Huangbo but had not yet reached the teaching, while Fayan Wenyi asks what a filial child should say and supplies a reply. A turning word can close or redirect an exchange, but possessing one successful line does not certify understanding.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes one arrowhead pierces three checkpoints in these Chan records. Its wording is ‘one arrowhead pierces three checkpoints.’ In Qinshan Wensui's exchange, Juliang asks what it is like when one arrow pierces three checkpoints; Qinshan answers, ‘release Qinshan Wensui within the checkpoints and let me see.’ After Juliang calls it a good arrow shot in the wrong place, Qinshan seizes him and says to set piercing three checkpoints aside and shoot an arrow for Qinshan; Juliang hesitates and is struck seven times. Yunmen gives the whole phrase as his own answer after asking how to undertake ‘covering heaven and earth, weighing the coming mechanism to the fraction’ without involving worldly conditions and receiving no answer from the assembly. Later teaching-seat records take up the same archery line with staffs, calling it a flash-like edge, and verse uses it as a closing line. The Zen bend is the military checkpoint-and-arrow formula's repeated use as an answer, challenge, and teaching-seat line in public encounter. The records do not define a universal set of three checkpoints here, so this entry does not substitute Huanglong's or Doushuai's named threes.

Senses.Explanation: In the records, ‘one eye’ is a figurative capacity used in appraisals: it may be possessed, placed, lost, exchanged, or opened, without the texts supplying a single assertion about what it sees. Literally "one" (一) classifier (隻) "eye" (眼): "one eye," attested 992 times in 233 allowlisted texts. The records use it in appraisals with the verbs possess, place, lose, exchange, and open. In the Damei case, Jiashan says, "at Damei I lost one eye" (我當時在大梅，失却一隻眼); Xuedou comments that Jiashan did not know he had then "exchanged for one eye" (換得一隻眼). Another appraisal says Yunmen "possesses only one eye" because he "only looks ahead and does not look behind" (只具一隻眼，只管瞻前，不管照後). Productive forms include "possess one eye" (具一隻眼, 476 occurrences), "place one eye here" (著得一隻眼, 89), "lose one eye" (失却一隻眼, 91), and "open another eye" (別開一隻眼).
Senses.Note: The phrase can expand beyond an individual appraisal. Xuefeng says, "the whole earth is a patch-robed monk's one eye" (盡大地是沙門一隻眼). Other instructions say that placing one eye at a cited point lets one "see seven ways vertically and eight ways horizontally" (便見七縱八橫), or that a staff "opens another eye" for the assembly. The corpus records these predicates and images without supplying a single replacement gloss for eye.

Senses.Explanation: The sixteen-foot golden body is the Buddha’s conventional majestic form, freely exchanged with a blade of grass in Chan transformation formulas. Chan repeatedly deploys it in a reversible formula: take one blade of grass and make it a sixteen-foot golden body, then make the golden body into one blade of grass. Other passages put the body on a refuse heap, ask directly 'what is the sixteen-foot golden body?' and answer with the administrative phrase 'the judge decides the case; the minister amends it,' or call it a mass of merit that is casually waved into the red dust. The Chan-specific bend is the contrast and reversibility: the exalted buddha-form is repeatedly exchanged with grass or located amid refuse and ordinary dust. These are the corpus's stated comparisons; the texts give no further gloss here.

Senses.Explanation: Thirty blows is a fixed counted beating assigned as a public verdict in Chan encounters and later comments. The sentence can arrive before action: Kaixian says it is due before crossing the teaching-hall gate, Dahui quotes its being due before stepping onto a boat, and Baoning makes movement itself incur it. It can also be retrospective or directed upward: Xuedou assigns it before Huineng reaches Caoxi, Nanjian has thirty blows for the World-Honored One, and Fohri Xi refuses to spare even one blow from earlier commentators. “I let you off with thirty blows” makes the sentence itself a pointed form of leniency in Jian Shan and Qingxi. Zen bends a conventional counted beating into a reusable teaching-seat judgement whose recipient may be monk, commentator, patriarch, or buddha.

Senses.Explanation: ‘Named condition’ is the selected English label for a borrowed name for a condition, command, or named mode that speakers say one enters, leaves, possesses, or displays. Its proper-name use instead identifies the named person Sanmei; that person/title referent is kept separate. The term occurs 4,852 times in 382 allowed texts. Huineng defines 'named condition of the single conduct' as 'at every place, while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, always carry one straight mind' (一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，常行一直心是也). The same address rejects the claim that 'not raising thought while constantly sitting unmoving is named condition of the single conduct' (常坐不動，妄不起心，即是一行三昧), saying that this understanding is like the insentient and blocks the Way. Mazu's record says that thought after thought becoming still is called 'named condition of the ocean seal,' which 'takes in all things as a hundred thousand different streams return together to the great sea' (喚作海印三昧攝一切法如百千異流同歸大海). It also says beings remain within 'named condition of the nature of the teaching' while dressing, eating, speaking, responding, using the six sense-roots, and carrying out every action (法性三昧中著衣喫飯言談祇對六根運用一切施為). Xuansha says that buddhas are people's 'self-receiving named condition' and that walking, standing, sitting, and lying down have never not been it; when asked what that named condition is, he replies, 'What use are so many modes of named condition?' (用如許多三昧作麼). The word therefore appears as the head of explicitly named states or domains whose predicates vary by text; this entry does not collapse those names into one imported definition.

Senses.Explanation: The three realms are mind-only: a received proposition that Chan records state, quote, and put under public test. Yongming Yanshou’s Record of the Source-Mirror quotes a scripture for the formula and pairs it with the myriad things being consciousness-only; the quoted document, not Yongming, utters the stored headword. Mazu Daoyi states it in his own address before saying that manifold appearances are stamped by one thing and that seen form is seeing mind. Yuanwu Keqin later attributes the same proposition to an unnamed old speaker and discusses the senses and consciousness. Xuansha Shibei asks Luohan Guichen how he understands it; Guichen points to a chair, and both call it wood. Dizang Guichen tells Fayan Wenyi that Fayan habitually states the paired formula, points to a courtyard stone, and asks whether it is inside or outside mind. Baoning Renyong states the pair before pointing to clouds, rain, stream water, and flowers and demanding that the source be investigated. The proposition remains one statement across exposition and encounter, while Zen bends it into chair, stone, and landscape tests rather than leaving it as an unchallenged formula.

Senses.Explanation: Xuansha Shibei's fixed case of three people: one blind, one deaf, and one unable to speak. His recorded challenge says that the blind person cannot see a raised mallet or whisk, the deaf person cannot hear spoken complete command, and the mute person cannot answer. Xuansha asks how elders claiming to receive people would receive them. The case record then has an unnamed participant ask permission to discuss the three, depart, and receive Xuansha's double rejection; Luohan Guichen turns the question onto Xuansha, who withdraws. Yunmen Wenyan later has a questioner bow, tests his movement, hearing, and answer, and the record reports a response. The exact phrase becomes portable case language: Yuanwu Keqin raises it in the Blue Cliff Record; Liao'an Qingyu raises the Yunmen handling; Yeweng Bo tells his visible assembly that they do not have the three impairments; and Tiantai Deshao answers a direct question with “you have just asked it.” Zen bends a medical triad into Xuansha's named public-interview case about receiving people when ordinary seeing, hearing, and answering are unavailable. The entry records the moves without supplying an unstated solution.

Senses.Explanation: A set of three tests, barriers, or checkpoint sayings, without one universal list. Wansong explicitly says that the label includes sets associated with Baizhang, Dayang, Puan, Linji, Xuansha, and the Old Pagoda master, and is not confined to Doushuai and Huanglong. In the separate formula 'one arrow pierces three checkpoints' (一鏃破三關), Qinshan is questioned about piercing three barriers and Yunmen supplies the same line as an answer after his assembly gives no answer. These are generic countable barriers; the two recurrent named taxonomies are separated below because their three questions refer to different things.

SearchAliases: three questions on nature and death
Senses.Explanation: Doushuai Congyue's three checkpoint sayings are a different fixed set. The first asks where one's nature is now when one parts the grass and looks to the wind only to see nature; the second asks how one escapes birth and death when the light of the eyes falls to the ground; the third asks where one goes when the four elements separate. Doushuai's record calls them 'three checkpoint sayings' (三關語) set up in the chamber to test students. A later public exchange invokes 'Doushuai's three-checkpoint sayings' and receives the invitation 'ask them one by one.' Their enumerated referents differ from Huanglong's buddha-hand, donkey-foot, and birth-circumstance questions.

Senses.Explanation: To descend from the teaching seat. In the Chan record this is the standard visible close of a formal teaching-seat appearance: the person who mounted the seat may finish speaking, shout, strike or plant an implement, remain silent, or answer a demand by leaving. The action is not interchangeable with the preceding speech. Shakyamuni Buddha descends after Manjusri's sounding-block declaration in one Five Lamps scene and after his own refusal to preach in another. Tianyi Yihuai shouts and descends; Feiyin Tongrong descends only after the chief seat gives the closing declaration; and Langting Jingting says of passing geese, “They have passed,” before descending. Yaoshan Weiyan mounts the seat, remains silent, descends, and only afterward answers the rector in his quarters. When Zhaozhou Congshen asks Nanquan Puyuan to speak apart from the four propositions and hundred negations, Nanquan descends and returns to his quarters. The Linji Yixuan–Mayu Baoche exchange makes the actors especially important: Mayu first pulls Linji down and takes the seat, Linji then pulls Mayu down and retakes it, and Linji finally descends after Mayu leaves. Juelang Daosheng is preparing to descend when a lay questioner introduced as Huang Gong tells him, “Please step down.” These formal endings, commands, and forcible removals all preserve the same concrete movement away from the seat.

Senses.Explanation: In the wild-fox case, 'not obscuring cause and effect' is Baizhang's turning answer; later comments question the fox's release and refuse to isolate it from the rejected companion phrase. The phrase occurs 150 times in 81 allowed texts, almost exactly alongside 'not falling into cause and effect' (不落因果, 151); the paired form 'not falling, not being blind' (不落不昧) occurs 86 times. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly contrasts the two phrases, while an unnamed monk inside the same commentary objects that even with 'not being blind to cause and effect' the fox body has not yet been shed. Dahui Zonggao preserves the paired questions but answers only by telling the questioner to raise them this way to people. Wumen Huikai asks why 'not falling' brought the fox body and why 'not being blind' shed it, then calls the pair 'two throws, one game' (不落不昧，兩采一賽). Chaozong Tongren rebukes both rejecting 'not falling' and clinging to 'not being blind' as tying oneself without a rope, yet continues by affirming 'not being blind to cause and effect' in his own stated frame. Later records continue asking whether the pair is the same or different. The records preserve competing deployments and questions; this entry does not select a winner among them.

Senses.Explanation: 不是心不是佛不是物 is ‘not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.’ The corpus transmits more than one explicit attribution: some witnesses introduce it with 故江西大師云 or report that 馬大師近日道 it, while the Nanquan–Zhaozhou case has 南泉云 or 南泉曰 before the same three-part formula. Senses.PreferredTarget: not be a companion to the myriad things
AlternateTargets: the one who is not a companion to the myriad things
SearchAliases: not companion to the ten thousand things

Senses.Explanation: Layman Pang’s fixed public question—who is not a companion of the ten thousand things?—is repeatedly raised afresh and answered in later records. Literally, not to be or become a companion to the myriad things. The expression is overwhelmingly recorded in the question, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' The Compendium of the Five Lamps records Layman Pang asking it first of Shitou Xiqian, who covers Pang's mouth, and later of Mazu Daoyi, who answers, 'When you swallow the West River in one mouthful, I will tell you.' Later masters quote Pang's question as a named public case, ask it afresh, and give their own answers. Letan Huaicheng answers 'Guanyin' (觀世音菩薩). Caoshan Benji answers, 'Where did all those many people in Hongzhou city go?' (汝道洪州城裏如許多人甚麼處去). Asked directly, 'Ultimately, what is not being a companion to the myriad things?' (畢竟如何是不與萬法為侶), Yinyuan Longqi answers, 'Passing through a hundred flowers, not one leaf clings to the body' (百花叢裏過，一葉不沾身). Xingkong Zhen answers another fresh raising with 'standing openly revealed' (堂堂獨露). Yuanwu Keqin's instruction says that the ancients called someone 'the person who is not a companion to the myriad things' (古人謂之不與萬法為侶底人). Zhang Jun's preface to Yuanwu's record says that whenever Yuanwu raised this public case, it was already dragging through mud and water and falling into the second meaning. The entry preserves the fixed wording, its named origin, and the answers that the record attaches to it.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase has 446 matches in 153 files. The person-question form has 139 matches in 73 files, while the longer nominal form ending in 'the one who' has 269 matches in 117. Three passages in three files directly ask, 'What is not being a companion to the myriad things?' One text explicitly calls it the public case of not being companion to the myriad things, and one instruction uses the naming formula 'the ancients called him the person who is not a companion to the myriad things.' The distribution supports one corpus-wide fixed expression rather than a meaning restricted to Layman Pang, Shitou, or Mazu.

Senses.Explanation: In Baizhang's wild-fox case, 'not falling into cause and effect' is the old man's fatal answer; later speakers repeatedly raise and question it against 'not obscuring cause and effect.' An old man who remained after Baizhang's addresses says that in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha he had lived on that mountain. A student asked him, “does a person of great conduct still fall into cause and effect or not?” He answered, “does not fall into cause and effect” (大修行底人還落因果也無？不落因果). The record says this answer was followed by five hundred lives in a wild-fox body. The old man asks Baizhang to give a substitute turning phrase; Baizhang answers, “does not obscure cause and effect” (不昧因果), and the old man awakens at the words. The record continues with the old man's request for a deceased monk's funeral and Huangbo's later question to Baizhang about the case. Wumen asks directly, “Not falling into cause and effect—why did he fall into a wild fox? Not obscuring cause and effect—why was he released from the wild fox?” (不落因果，為甚墮野狐？不昧因果，為甚脫野狐？). Wansong retells the same speaker turns in his commentary. A later master questions a student on the stated difference between falling and not obscuring, while an earlier lamp dialogue rebukes the cited participant's “then it does not fall into cause and effect” with “do not make a wild-jackal cry” (莫作野干鳴). The exact phrase occurs 151 times in 82 allowlisted files. A later record preserves two unnamed monks disputing the case: one says that 'not obscuring' still did not shed the fox body, while the other asks how 'not falling' ever incurred it. Chaozong's record also has an unnamed monk publicly ask why 'not falling into cause and effect' led to the fox. These are distinct later interrogations of the same case phrase, not new senses.

In the central case, Qingfeng Chuanhong answers a question about the student's own self with the fire-stem boy coming to seek fire. The unnamed questioner explains the line as fire seeking fire and oneself seeking oneself; Fayan Wenyi rejects that explanation, repeats the same answer when questioned, and the record says the questioner awakened. The figure then travels beyond case narration while retaining overt fire settings: Hengchuan Rukong answers a furnace-opening challenge with leafy firewood; Muyun Tongmen invokes the boy while dropping a funeral torch; and Xutang calls to him in another torch address. The phrase therefore becomes an exact case answer, case label, and fire-ceremony address. SearchAliases: Danxia's burning of the wooden buddha
Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes Danxia burns the wooden buddha in these Chan records. Its wording is ‘Danxia burns a buddha’; in the narrated case the referent is explicitly a wooden buddha-image. Frozen-corpus concordance: 14 exact hits in 8 storage files representing 8 independent works. The repeated account says that, finding it cold at Huilin monastery, Danxia Tianran took a wooden buddha and burned it for a fire. When the temple officer rebuked him for burning ‘my wooden buddha,’ Danxia stirred the ashes with his staff and said he was looking for relics. The officer answered that a wooden buddha has no relics; Danxia then requested two more images to burn. The record adds that afterward the officer's eyebrows and beard fell out. Later masters preserve this as a numbered public case, ask whether Danxia's own eyebrows remain, warn against denying cause and effect, and group it in one roster with Manjusri holding the sword, Guizong cutting the snake, and Muzhou shutting the door. One later verse explicitly calls the deed ‘not light,’ mentions the officer's facial hair, and says that what one does one receives. These are the corpus's narrated actions and comments; this entry does not acquit or condemn Danxia.

Senses.Explanation: In Linji’s guest–host scheme, guest within host is the configuration explicitly defined by “the teaching figure lacks a nose-hole.” In the Linji-house definition preserved by The Eye of Humans and Gods, the teaching figure having a ‘nose-hole’ is host-within-host, the student having one is host-within-guest, the teaching figure lacking one is guest-within-host, and the student lacking one is guest-within-guest; the compilation immediately warns that this differs from Caodong guest-and-host. That explicit definition makes ‘guest within host’ (主中賓) here the position in which ‘the teaching figure lacks a nose-hole; this is named guest within host’ (師家無鼻孔，名主中賓), rather than a free synonym for the whole guest-host pair. The same compilation records the term as a question answered by Fengxue (‘the returning simurgh, the two luminaries renewed’), as a verse heading, and in several masters' complete four-position catechisms. Later records continue asking ‘what is guest within host?’ and answer with fresh lines such as ‘green mountains cover white clouds’ and ‘empty-handed, mingling with the dusty world.’ The changing answers remain answers to one named public-interview position; this entry reports them without choosing a hidden interpretation.

Senses.Explanation: The ordinary title for a household’s person in charge becomes a personified designation tested in Chan self-address, questions, equations, and corrections. A compiler narrates Ruiyan Shiyan’s daily calling to the one in charge and self-response; another record quotes the call directly. Dongshan Liangjie asks which one is his interlocutor’s person in charge and rejects the readily responding person as an answer. Tianru Weize explicitly says that mind, on each person’s own share, is called oneself and also the one in charge. Zhongfeng Mingben groups Ruiyan’s designation with Linji Yixuan’s true person of no rank, while Yulin Tongxiu warns against taking bright identity-consciousness as realization of it. Zhaozhou Congshen says it is no other person and warns against seeking outside. The label therefore functions as something called, located, equated, and tested, not as an unexamined modern theory of self.

Senses.Explanation: A dry shit-stick is the latrine wiping-tool named by the compound. Linji Yixuan asks what dry shit-stick the person of no rank is; Deshan Xuanjian predicates it of old Shakyamuni; and Yunmen Wenyan asks what dry shit-stick an assembly seeks to chew. In Yunmen’s famous case it answers ‘What is Buddha?’ Wumen Huikai preserves Yunmen as the answerer, Dahui Zonggao repeats the case in verse, and Zhongfeng Mingben places it beside the courtyard cypress and three catties of hemp as sayings with no route for explanatory boring. Wanpu Zhao later asks Miyun Yuanwu what it is and receives only ‘Look on the field ridge.’ The records deploy the named wiping-tool in questions, predicates, answers, case titles, and commentary; they assign it no further stable gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Compound/object control follows the guide’s calibration: dry + excrement + stick names the latrine wiping-tool, while the corpus does not warrant claims about a particular material construction or a menu of symbolic readings. Seven exact witnesses from seven distinct works.

Senses.Explanation: Taking away neither person nor environment is one member of Linji’s Four Selections, stated as a rubric and answered through fresh images. The fourth member of Linji's four statements later called the Four Selections: ‘at times, take away neither the person nor the surroundings.’ In Linji's own record it appears as one member of the complete four and immediately becomes a public question. Asked ‘what is taking away neither person nor surroundings?’ Linji answers, ‘the king ascends the jeweled hall; the rustic elder sings.’ The record does not explain the formula beyond that exchange. Later collections preserve Linji's wording, attach Kefu's verse—beginning ‘thought does not incline to either side; guest and host differ little; question and answer are both complete’—and invite many later masters to answer the same named question with new lines, including Fengxue's ‘the emperor remembers: in the third month south of the river, amid the partridge's cry the hundred flowers are fragrant.’ The formula circulates as a case heading, verse heading, and recurring public-interview question.

Senses.Explanation: One of Linji Yixuan's four named selections: the member whose wording says that both the person and the encountered scene are taken away. Linji's own record places it after taking away only the person and taking away only the scene, and before taking away neither; the four are roster alternatives, not a report of two physical objects disappearing. In Eyes of Humans and Gods, a reviewed unnamed monk asks Linji about this member, and Linji answers with news from Bing and Fen being cut off and one quarter standing alone. Later reviewed unnamed monks ask Yuanwu Keqin, Feiyin Tongrong, and Jie'an Wujin the same public question. Yuanwu answers ‘gather in,’ paired with ‘let out’ for taking away neither; Feiyin asks where the questioner can establish a body; Jie'an answers once that deliberation is a thousand miles away and elsewhere orders the questioner to take a beating twice. Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes Linji's complete four-member roster and publicly asks which member Tianyin's own shout enacts. These named responses preserve a recurring public question and a Linji-house selection, but their incompatible answers do not supply one hidden definition of person or scene.

Senses.Explanation: To entrust is to place the teaching, community, or named responsibility in another's care through an explicit charge. Records use it for Buddha entrusting the treasury to Kasyapa and for later lineage and institutional charges.

Entries.CreatedBy: Codex fresh-build lane C

Senses.Explanation: The term names the act or formula of entrusting the teaching from an entrusting predecessor to a successor: literally ‘entrust’ (付) the ‘teaching’ (法), attested 608 times in 143 allowlisted texts. Lamp records use it for a predecessor handing the teaching to a successor. Layman Shi Zhicheng's ninth question summarizes the lineage claim as ‘after the Buddha's extinction, the teaching was entrusted to Kasyapa and mind was transmitted by mind’ (佛滅後付法於迦葉，以心傳心). Narrative closure frequently says ‘after the patriarch had entrusted the teaching’ (祖付法已), followed by his departure or death. The compound ‘verse on entrusting the teaching’ (付法偈) names verses spoken or recorded at that handover.
Senses.Note: The verses themselves often question the wording of transmission. One early verse says, "originally a teaching was entrusted; after entrusting it, [one] says there is no teaching; each must awaken for oneself; once awakened, there is no no-teaching" (本來付有法，付了言無法，各各須自悟，悟了無無法). A later preface asks why transmission verses are recorded for earlier buddhas and patriarchs but not below Mazu: was there no entrustment, or was it kept from disclosure? Another instruction ranks a thousand who have opened up below one person entrusted with the teaching, and a thousand entrusted below one who goes out into the world. These are text-stated comparisons within the same verb sense.

Senses.Explanation: To take its own course or proceed without forced direction. The compound occurs 1,101 times in 250 allowlisted texts. Yuanwu Keqin gives an explicit comparison: 'what is called proceeding of itself is like a dull-witted person whose household has a capable person caring for him.' Other records pair it with following circumstances in both word orders, with freedom, and with the doubled expansion 'buoyantly proceeding of itself.' Concrete lines place it after drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry, or say that at all times and places one proceeds of oneself freely and responds without a fixed direction. Zen bends an ordinary course-running expression into descriptions of conduct and response, but the evidence does not turn it into passivity or one uniform instruction.
Senses.Note: The doubled expansion 'buoyantly proceeding of itself' occurs 140 times in 94 texts. 'Proceed of itself and follow circumstances' and its reverse each occur 27 times; 'proceed of itself freely' occurs five times in five texts. This predicate is distinct from the exact title of the seventh oxherding section recorded below.

Senses.Explanation: The doubled command tells someone to rest, cease, and settle; later speakers quote it, criticize fixed adherence to it, or refuse both it and its negation. Chan records preserve it both as Shishuang Qingzhu's compact sequence of stilling images and as a disputed formula: Yunfeng Wenyue reverses it, Yulin Tongxiu refuses both alternatives, and Dahui Zonggao and Zhongfeng Mingben criticize inert or formulaic applications. Shishuang Qingzhu's recorded sequence expands it: "rest; cease; let one thought last ten thousand years; become cold ashes and a withered tree; become an incense burner in an old shrine; become one strip of white silk; become cold and still" (休去歇去、一念萬年去、寒灰枯木去、古廟香爐去、一條白練去、冷秋秋地去). Yunfeng Wenyue supplies a contrary sequence beginning "do not rest and do not cease" (不休不歇去), and Yulin Tongxiu says that neither resting-and-ceasing nor not-resting-and-not-ceasing is permitted (也不許休去歇去，也不許不休不歇去). Dahui Zonggao reports people sitting slack-jawed and calling that "resting and ceasing" (一向嘴盧都地打坐，謂之休去歇去), in an extended criticism. Zhongfeng Mingben likewise reports people citing "do not fantasize, put it down, old-shrine incense burner, rest and cease" as evidence, and compares that use to waiting by a stump for a rabbit. Other records retain the literal instruction: Yunmen Wenyan says, "from now on, rest; cease" (自今以往，休去歇去), while Dafang Yin asks, "why not rest and cease?" (何不休去歇去). The entry records the command, its stock sequence, its contrary, and the corpus's criticisms; it does not turn the words into a prescribed system.

Senses.Explanation: The two graphs overlap in stopping and resting: 'rest,' 'cease,' or 'come to rest.' The allowlisted record has 801 occurrences in 215 storage files. The word functions as a verb in imperatives such as 'go rest' (休歇去), as a predicate in questions such as 'have you yet found rest?' (還得個休歇也未), and as an attributive noun in 'a resting place' (休歇處) and 'ground of rest' (休歇地). Linji Yixuan says, 'better to be without concerns and go rest; hungry, eat; tired, close your eyes' (不如無事休歇去，飢來喫飯，困來合眼). Qingyuan Weixin says that after first seeing mountains as mountains, then not as mountains, he had now 'found a resting place' and again saw mountains simply as mountains and waters as waters (而今得箇休歇處，依然見山秖是山，見水秖是水). Zishou Chuyan asks what the resting place is and answers, 'when cold, sit around the stove; when at leisure, sleep as one pleases' (寒則圍爐座，閑時任性眠). Fayan Wenyi counters a monk's question with 'what did you get that you do not rest?' (汝得箇什麼即不休歇去). Zhenxie Qingliao rejects making a resting place out of dwelling in empty stillness and guarding the lifelessness before a dead tree, saying that this 'has no connection' (沒交涉). Zen therefore bends ordinary rest into a questioned and publicly tested resting place while preserving eating, sleeping, and stove-sitting as its plain-language control.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 801 hits in 215 storage files. Attested formations include 'go rest,' 118/61; 'resting place,' 71/53; 'great rest,' 72/44; doubled 'stop and rest,' 158/80; 'have [you] rested yet?,' 7/7; and 'ground of rest,' 11/9. The single older-index 'is called a resting place' occurrence is Zhenxie Qingliao's rejection of that label, not his endorsement. The single person-marker construction asks why ancestral teachers sought people's rest; it is a question, not a self-definition.

Senses.Explanation: The matter beyond a buddha is a stock public-interview formula for what remains when even 'buddha' is treated as a position one can ask beyond. Dongshan Liangjie says it must be known before one has a share in speech and answers a request for it with 'not buddha.' Yushan Shangsi repeats that consequence, Dahui Zonggao tells his audience to set the formula aside before enacting a staff answer, and named and unnamed monastics pose it as a question. The witnesses show a deliberately recurrent question-position and divergent responses; they do not license a single hidden answer.

SearchAliases: does a dog have buddha nature
Senses.Explanation: Buddha-nature is an inherited category that the Chan record turns into a contested public claim rather than leaving as a settled possession. Named speakers say that all sentient beings have it and that none have it; Hongren denies it to a southerner, while Huineng answers that it does not follow north and south. Secretary Zhu asks where it is when both halves of a cut earthworm move, and an unnamed participant asks Nagarjuna about its size. Baizhang Huaihai describes a failure to see it, while Dahui Zonggao raises Yongjia Xuanjue's verse containing it. The same headword is affirmed, denied, located, questioned, missed, and raised for later scrutiny; this entry records that range without supplying a metaphysical substance behind the word.

Senses.Explanation: “The essential point of Buddha’s teaching” is a stock public-interview question whose force lies in demanding a present answer, not in supplying a settled propositional formula. Monks and officials put the same question to Budai, Daolin, Linji, Qingliang, and Xuedou; the respondents put down a bag, quote an elementary moral maxim, shout, defer the question, or offer an image. The stable lexical unit is the demand for the teaching’s main point. Zen bends it by making the answer an event of the interview rather than a reusable definition.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Yulin, complete birthday hall address: Yulin Tongxiu tells the assembly that each of them walks atop the crowns of buddhas and patriarchs, then calls for anyone not deceived to come forward.

Senses.Explanation: Buddhas and patriarchs is the corpus's paired authority formula, not a claim that the two are historically identical. Rui'an Sengyin opposes the pair to a demonic army in his death verse; Baichi Yuanshuo and Mingjue Cong invoke their inherited teaching; Huqiu Shaolong says their arrangements have no place in his gate; and Yulin Tongxiu speaks of treading on their crowns. The phrase thus names the established religious and lineage authorities that speakers inherit, invoke, reject as an arrangement, or publicly overtop. Two former witnesses were removed because their text was actually 佛 followed across a turn boundary by 祖云, 'the patriarch said,' not the headword 佛祖.

Senses.Explanation: The term credits or tests demonstrated competence: an adept, a real hand. Yuanwu Keqin applies it to an interlocutor who handles an exchange, to an adept lineage teacher who frees people from entanglement, to a meeting conducted on adept terms, and to an adept Chan guest who acts as soon as a case is raised. Pang Yun exclaims it as direct praise. Xinghua Cunjiang compounds it with battle-general and demands a direct advance. Qingping Weikuang dismisses the approaching participant as not an adept. In a poetic exchange an unnamed interlocutor uses it with poet, showing that the competence belongs to the role supplied by context rather than defining only a Chan office. The corpus supports expert status, not the modern default sense author or writer. Independent later witnesses apply it to the means required of a teaching-seat master and even to Emperor Zhuangzong as an ‘adept ruler’; the competence follows the supplied role. A corpus-wide control for the ordinary verbs ‘compose,’ ‘write,’ and ‘compile,’ the ordinary noun ‘author,’ and the compound ‘adept poet’ found author/composer grammar named by other words, while the headword continues to predicate demonstrated capability.
Senses.Note: Ten exact witnesses across six distinct works. Occupational/author controls were actively tested; no curated line requires modern ‘author/writer’ as the bare-headword referent.

Senses.Explanation: This interrogative asks how something is, how one will respond, or what can be said or done: “how?” Its force is often a live demand rather than a request for exposition. Baizhang Huaihai blocks throat and lips and asks how Guishan will speak; Shitou Xiqian rejects “this way” and “not this way” and asks what his student will do; Linji Yixuan asks how the present listener proposes to cultivate, realize, or adorn the person hearing the teaching. It also follows a proposed action—“what if the foot is raised?”—asks how someone understands a case, presses “ultimately, how?”, asks how a ceremonial address should be raised, or introduces “what is the final phrase?” Dialectal spellings perform the same interrogative work in the stored witnesses. The phrase supplies no answer by itself; its recurring role is to force the next move.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 29,839 hits in 443 files and 436 works. Ten curated occurrences cover personal, modal, interpretive, ceremonial, and case-question frames.

Senses.Explanation: How do you understand it? A recurrent public-interview question put to an individual or the whole assembly after a saying, action, quotation, or case has been raised. Linji Yixuan asks how an unnamed participant understands the four stated uses of a shout and answers the participant’s hesitation with a shout. Wufeng Ziqi asks, ‘How do you understand it?’ (你作麼生會); the unnamed respondent shouts, and Wufeng says ‘not yet’ (未在) before asking what comes after one shout or two. In a whisk case, Ganzi Xingzhe asks how a visitor understands Guishan Lingyou’s intention in raising the whisk; the offered account is rejected with ‘You had better return to Guishan’ (且歸溈山去好). Cuiyan Shouzhi says that National Teacher Huizhong and his attendant both still lacked understanding and asks, ‘How do you understand it now?’ (如今作麼生會). Yunju Shun similarly reopens the Puyan–Samantabhadra case for the assembly. The phrase demands an answer that can itself be answered, rejected, or tested in public; the texts do not define it as silent inward comprehension.

Senses.Explanation: “How do you say it?”—a direct demand for words in a recorded Zen public interview. Frozen-corpus concordance: 3680 exact hits in 334 storage files representing 330 independent works. Baizhang Huaihai asks Guishan Lingyou, “with throat and lips shut, how do you say it?” (併却咽喉唇吻，作麼生道); Baizhang then puts the same demand to Wufeng and Yunyan. Records also use it to demand “a phrase not involving the teaching framework” (不涉化門一句), “a phrase not falling into words” (不落言詮), or an answer from the respondent's own breast. In retrospective questions, it asks how a named earlier teacher spoke: “how did Jingshan say it to you?” (徑山向汝作麼生道). Zen bends an ordinary wording question into a public demand for an accountable spoken response. Direct and retrospective forms change subject and tense, not the thing being asked.

Senses.Explanation: “Still unchanged from before” marks that an answer, condition, or mistake remains as it was despite the preceding exchange. Something is described by this expression when a new turn, label, recognition, or interval leaves it still unchanged from before. Deng Yinfeng goes back and asks Shitou Xiqian the same question again; a reviewed unnamed monk reaches Xuefeng Yicun and repeats Zhaozhou Congshen's instructed reply exactly as before. Fenyang Shanzhao says that recognizing the nature as one's own mind is still not it, while Datian Baotong says that the blind remain blind and the mute remain mute. Zhenxie Qingliao says that calculation fails and one remains embarrassed as before. Qingyuan Weixin describes first seeing mountains and waters ordinarily, then seeing them otherwise, and finally seeing mountains only as mountains and waters only as waters again as before. Dahui Zonggao says that calling someone a bodhisattva or a thief may produce pleasure or anger, yet the person remains the same old person. Deshan Jingzhao'an Zongshi holds up a fly whisk and says that calling it a fly whisk is still not it, while not calling it one is deliberate failure to recognize it. These actors use one ordinary adverb for repeated conduct and continuing states, and also bend it into a recurrent interview verdict: the attempted answer, recognition, calculation, or relabeling has changed nothing.

Senses.Explanation: Baichi Yuan makes the wording concrete: after saying 'draw a gourd following the model,' he traces a circle with his hand and says, 'this is the model for the gourd.' Chan records most often use the idiom to appraise copied words or conduct in public exchanges. When a student repeats the form of an earlier answer, Gulin Qingmao calls it drawing a gourd from the model and rebukes him. Another record explicitly denies that its handling of an old case is following another's heels or drawing a gourd from the model. A later address applies the phrase across famous lineage gestures: the Buddha holding up the flower, Bodhidharma facing the wall, Linji's shout, and Deshan's staff are followed by descendants who 'each draw a gourd following the model.' The Zen deviation is this ordinary craft-copying idiom used to audit repeated case answers, gestures, verses, and recorded lineages. Since masters also use it self-referentially, the phrase is not condemnation by definition.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase occurs 128 times in 71 allowlisted texts. Chan masters repeatedly apply the plant-clinging image as a rebuke. Ying'an Tanhua lists striking the bench, raising the whisk, blinking, raising the eyebrows, pointing east and west, and moving the lips and tongue, then says that these still do not escape clinging to grass and attaching to trees. Chijue Daochong applies it to making a livelihood on circumstances and objects and seeking clever explanations in principle and nature. Yuanwu Keqin calls people who talk of gain and loss ‘spirits clinging to grass and attaching to trees’ (說得說失得麼。若有恁麼。盡是依草附木精靈). In his case commentary, Yuanwu sets the phrase alongside feeling along a fence and wall, while Gulin Qingmao calls an interlocutor's raised fist precisely such clinging. The bearer can be called a spirit or a person, and the criticized support changes with the passage; the headword still names the same act of dependence.

Senses.Explanation: “Then descended from the seat” records the immediate close of a hall appearance after a statement, gesture, exchange, or ceremonial dedication. Literally, "then descended from the seat" . In Chan records this is a formal scene-closing action tied to the high teaching seat, not merely someone sitting down or leaving ordinary furniture. The Buddha cases make the institutional structure explicit: the Buddha mounts the seat , the assembly settles, Manjusri or Kasyapa strikes the sounding block and announces the king of teachings' teaching or that the talk is finished, and the Buddha then descends. The phrase can close a spoken address after a final question, as when Linji tells the assembly to ask the two hall leaders about host and guest and descends. It also closes action without a final speech: after Magu exits during the exchange of seats, Linji descends. In the Mazu-Baizhang encounter, Baizhang rolls up the mat as soon as Mazu mounts the hall, and Mazu descends and continues the exchange in his quarters. The distinctive Chan deployment is the visible termination of the formal teaching-seat event; sometimes the descent itself is the entire recorded close.

Senses.Explanation: “Juzhi’s One Finger” names Juzhi’s recurrent public gesture and the case that includes Tianlong, Juzhi, and the attendant boy. The Lamp Record supplies the narrative behind the label: Tianlong showed Juzhi one raised finger; thereafter Juzhi raised one finger to visiting monks; when a boy copied him, Juzhi cut off the boy's finger, called him back, and raised his own finger. Later records place ‘Juzhi's one finger’ beside Xuefeng's rolling ball, Yunmen's looking-and-‘look!,’ Muzhou's ‘ready-made,’ Deshan's staff, and Linji's shout as a named response associated with Yuanwu Keqin. Verses call it ‘one-finger Chan,’ say it was used throughout Juzhi's life, and repeatedly ask or comment on where he was accurate. The entry reports the gesture, its narrative, and its later case-label use; the texts do not supply a further gloss for what the finger denotes.

Senses.Explanation: Qiannu's soul leaves her body. In Chan records this phrase is the title and shorthand of a public case built around Wuzu Fayan's question: Qiannu's soul departed—which one is real? Wumen preserves the question and warns against running about wildly in his comment. Fojian Huiqin repeatedly presses Cishou Huaishen with the case until the record says an obstruction opened. Fuyan Ya discusses it with a lay official and warns him not to fasten onto Qiannu. Xueguan Zhiyin keeps the case open through its own alternatives: whether she is karmic consciousness or mind-born, and whether one or two; his answer says there is no need to display form and shadow. Chaozong Tongren answers the real-one question with two strikes and a warning against eloping. Baishan Dekai answers a layperson's version with ‘where money was lost in the river, dredge in the river.’ The tale-name has become a compact, repeatedly interviewed case formula. The entry reports the questions and answers without selecting a real Qiannu for them.

Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, the rank “absolute within the relative” (偏中正) names the absolute or upright disclosed within the relative or differentiated, reversing the nesting of “relative within the absolute” while remaining paired with it in explanations and verse sequences. Caoshan Benji glosses the rank as leaving affairs and entering principle. The Eyes of Humans and Devas transmits the same affairs-to-principle gloss in its Five Ranks account. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives the rank a sea-cloud, sacred-peak, returning-traveler, and mirror image. Langting Ting pairs it with a yellow bird carrying spring news. Juelang Daosheng associates it with a western circle and lesser yin, while Ruibai Mingxue identifies the same shout as this rank when it is silent right where it occurs. Tianran Hanshi reports Dongshan's old-woman-and-mirror stanza and answers it with another mirror verse; the varied images illustrate rather than define the relation.

Senses.Explanation: Layman Fu is an invoked pre-lineage figure defined by his deployment in Chan records. Yuanwu Keqin raises the public case in which Emperor Wu invites Layman Fu to lecture on the Diamond Scripture; Fu strikes the desk and leaves the seat, and Zhigong says that the lecture is finished. Guishan Gumei raises another Emperor Wu case in which Fu arrives wearing a Buddhist robe, a Daoist cap, and Confucian shoes; questioned in turn about a monastic, Daoist, or Confucian identity, Fu points respectively to the cap, shoes, and robe (披衲 / 頂冠 / 靸履). The same Blue Cliff Record passage identifies him as living at Yunhuang Mountain, planting two trees called the Twin Grove, and calling himself the future Layman Shanhui. Later masters quote and test him rather than merely preserve biography. Pin Jixiang raises Fu's full verse: 'Night after night I sleep embracing Buddha; morning after morning I rise together with him. Sitting and rising we constantly follow each other; in speech and silence we dwell together. Not separated by the slightest hair, we are like body and shadow. If you wish to know where Buddha goes, it is only this voice' (夜夜抱佛眠，朝朝還共起，起坐鎮相隨，語默同居止，些毫不相離，如身影相似，欲識佛去處，只者語聲是). Fatai criticizes the verse's final line. Foyan Qingyuan's citation of Fu's Heart-King Inscription—salt's taste in water and blue pigment in color—appears in Baiyang Fashun's awakening account. Yina Jie inscribes Fu's portrait as neither Confucian, Daoist, nor Chan. A Chan old-case collection explicitly attributes to Fu the verse, 'Empty-handed, holding a hoe; walking on foot, riding a water buffalo; a person crosses over a bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not' (空手把鋤頭，步行騎水牛，人從槗上過，槗流水不流). Doushuai Congyue says Fu only knew washing while holding a bridge pillar and releasing a boat. Zhongfeng Mingben discusses Fu's voice saying, and Tianyin Yuanxiu raises and questions the lecture case. Thus the Zen Fu is lecturer-who-strikes-and-leaves, mixed-attire interlocutor, quoted author, verse speaker, portrait subject, and target of later public criticism.

Senses.Explanation: The records use ‘transmit the lamp’ for teacher-to-successor continuation, drawing the continuation through lamp and flame equations. Literally, transmit the lamp. The expression uses one lamp lighting the next for continuation from teacher to successor. Records pair it with continuing the flame, say that lamp follows lamp and ancestor transmits to ancestor, and ask what is being continued. The preface to the Jingde Record explicitly calls it 'the comparison of transmitting the lamp.' A later preface gives its own intensified definition: 'transmitting the lamp is transmitting this hot flame.' That hot-flame equation belongs to that preface's five-lamps discussion and is not imposed on every occurrence.

Senses.Explanation: This recurring recorder formula introduces a question by an unidentified monastic and hands the next turn to a named respondent. It can open a famous case, introduce another question in an ongoing record, or appear with modifiers such as “there was,” “again,” and “at the time.” The stored passages range from questions about a dog’s buddha-nature, the central meaning of the teaching, the ancestral teacher’s coming from the west, a singular matter, the price of rice, what the respondent is doing in the street, and the gate of absence of division. The first graph identifies the questioning participant as a monastic and the second marks the question event. Because none of the ten questioners is personally named after full passage and parallel review, the entry does not assign them masters’ names merely from the respondent or section owner. The four previously orphaned respondents are Oxhead Zhiwei, Helin Xuansu, Budai Qici, and Tianyi Yihuai; they answer the questions but do not utter the recorder formula.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 31,994 hits in 437 files representing 431 independent works. Ten curated occurrences from ten independent works meet the high-frequency floor.

Zen at the gate of light and shadow
Senses.Explanation: The gate of light and shadow is the records' visible threshold contrasted with the matter inside the house: people mistake its coarse, shallow business for what is within (光影門頭戶底麤淺底事，將作屋裏事). Elsewhere Xueguan Zhiyin says students "recognize only the gate of light and shadow as themselves" (惟認光影門頭當作自己). The phrase also enters verse as a place not to stop: "do not halt your steps at the gate of light and shadow" (光影門頭休駐足). Hongzhi supplies a notable counter-deployment: "a person who settles the matter at the gate of light and shadow will do" (光影門頭了事底漢即得), then immediately asks how one proceeds before guest and host divide and before an image is formed. Zen thus bends ordinary light, shadow, and doorway language into a recurring label for the visible or reflected threshold that records contrast with the inside of the house, oneself, and the not-yet-formed image.

Senses.Explanation: To enter settled absorption is to settle into an absorbed, composed state from which someone may later emerge. Sanghanandi sits in settled absorption for twenty-one days and then rises; the reviewed unnamed woman in the famous public case remains in settled absorption when Manjusri cannot bring her out. Zhirong asks Zhihuang whether he enters with mind or without mind. When Zhihuang says that during settled absorption he sees neither a present nor an absent mind, Zhirong replies that constant settled absorption should have no further entry or exit. Mazu Daoyi classifies observing emptiness and entering settled absorption as contrivance. Baizhang Huaihai says not to take settled absorption and enter settled absorption, just as one should not take Chan and think about Chan or take buddha and seek buddha. An unnamed monk asks Liuhe Xiangji Zi what an unnamed monk in settled absorption is, and Xiangji answers that the four seas are originally limpid. Yongming Yanshou criticizes merely leaving thought to enter settled absorption while rejecting objects to seek truth. These named challenges do not erase the visible state and its entry-and-emergence grammar; they are where the Chan record repeatedly tests it.
Senses.Note: This reversible-state sense is independently established by sitting, remaining, questioning, entering, and later emerging. Yongming Yanshou quotes an outside treatise that defines entry through seeing a speck's nature as empty and the true principle of the ten directions; because Yongming explicitly identifies that outside framework, it is inventoried but not substituted for the encounter-record description. The lineage-biography death-notice use is separated below because its dated terminal event is a different thing from a state followed by emergence. The dated terminal notices use the same entered settled state followed by death; they are retained as a deployment of this sense, not split as another lexical event.

Senses.Explanation: In Chan records it is a stock description of a recorded teacher becoming involved in words, teaching, or an encounter for others. One passage expressly calls the interlocked condition 'gain within no-gain and no-gain within gain' entering mud and water, then pairs it with 'ride the thief's horse and pursue the thief's band.' Before an assembly Guanghui Yuanlian says that he does not avoid others' scrutiny and enters mud and water 'for you people'; Songyuan Chongyue's record places the phrase as his answer in a numbered question-and-answer sequence. A historical contrast says that at Magadha the edge was already exposed and before Shaoshi Peak Bodhidharma 'entered mud and water.' The Zen deviation is this repeated use of ordinary muddy immersion for the teaching-seat act of entering entangling speech and encounters for an audience; the texts also criticize particular instances, so the phrase is not praise by definition.

Senses.Explanation: To enter the sea and count its sand is to undertake an immense enumeration that cannot deliver the thing sought. Huanglong Huinan pairs the image with reciting phrases and recognizing reflected light; Tian'an Sheng quotes the complaint that studying names and forms became sand-counting and counting another's treasure. Guxue Zhe applies it to extensive pilgrimage, while Chaozong Tongren lists classificatory schemes and interpretation as unable to reach the matter. Yuan'an Feng says a mistaken vision leaves later people counting sea-sand. Chan usage targets exhaustive accumulation that remains external to the immediate case.

Senses.Explanation: To present in full is to bring the whole matter forward without leaving a remainder; the phrase appears in questions, answers, and appraisals of complete presentation. Literally, to raise or present in full. Yunmen Wenyan supplies the decisive contrast: seeing no single form is only half-presentation, and even then one must know the occasion of full presentation . Shengyin Chongkai pairs presentation across past and present with the ancestral master's true command . Juelang Dasheng joins the flower at Vulture Peak and snow at Shaoshi with separate transmission personally shown and the true command fully presented . Yuanwu Keqin raises the command in full and publicly asks how it can be unfolded. Liao'an Qingyu says that the entrustment at Vulture Peak is precisely here and tells the assembly to take up one fully presented saying ; Shending Yunwai Ze similarly says that if one can present it whole with bare hands, ease is assured . Zen bends the ordinary sense of completeness toward teaching-seat language: a saying, command, or lineage entrustment is brought forward without remainder and submitted to the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: The whole dynamic or full pivotal function: the complete working of a trigger or pivot. The graphs join ‘whole or complete’ (全) to ‘trigger, pivot, or dynamic’ (機). The compound has 948 occurrences in 244 allowlisted texts. It is especially visible in ‘the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用). Yuanwu Keqin says this ‘whole dynamic and great function is manifest wherever one touches’ (全機大用觸處見成); elsewhere his record says ‘as the grass bends and the wind moves, the whole dynamic alone is exposed’ (草偃風行全機獨露), then asks what one says without relying on any thing or phrase. Yuanwu also speaks of the whole dynamic ‘alone functioning’ (全機獨用). Chaozong Tongren pairs a wisdom-sword cutting bonds with the whole dynamic ‘thoroughly freed’ (全機透脫), then immediately glosses being freed as a sick person finally sweating. The Blue Cliff Record uses the term both in Yuanwu's case pointer ‘the whole dynamic is displayed everywhere’ (全機隨處齊彰) and in his comment that several actions are all ‘places of the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用處). Gongchen Daoxian uses the compound predicatively: ‘if I deploy the whole dynamic, where will you search?’ (我若全機，汝向甚麼處摸索). The records thus bend an ordinary word for the complete working of a mechanism into language for undivided operation at the teaching seat.
Senses.Note: The sole construction with the nominalizing person-marker (者) describes a person who broadly displayed the whole dynamic; it does not define a second sense. In Shiguan Fazang's autobiographical record, his teacher Juelang Daosheng asks ‘what is the whole dynamic?’ (如何是全機), and Shiguan answers by raising one finger; when asked about the whole function, he spreads both hands. The former entry incorrectly attached an unrelated ‘midnight sun’ answer to this exchange; exact KWIC review removes that error. The same referent spans direct discourse, case rubrics, verse, and prose comment, so neither grammatical variation nor different speakers warrant a second sense.

Senses.Explanation: A public case is a recorded encounter or saying set before students as an authoritative test object. Zhongfeng Mingben explicitly compares it to a government office's case documents and says that a lineage teacher raises one to decide an unsettled student's understanding. Sanjiao Laoren says patriarchs established such records and left them for the monasteries. Wumen Huikai uses old public cases as tiles for knocking on the gate; Yuanwu Keqin says later people gave this name to the old teachers' occasion-matched pointers. Later records warn against dissecting every old case for a fixed route, renew an old case in present interview, and call an immediately present encounter a ready-made case. The legal comparison explains the authority and adjudicative force of the Chan record-object without reducing it to a secular lawsuit.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 4,375 hits in 393 files and 387 works. Eight exact witnesses across six independent works cover definition, adjudication, institutional preservation, pedagogical use, retrospective naming, misuse, renewal, and immediate deployment.

SearchAliases: at the gates of the six faculties
at the gateways of the six faculties
Senses.Explanation: The phrase locates activity at the six sensory gateways—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—where seeing, hearing, sensing, and thought meet their objects. Chan speakers point to these ‘gate-fronts’ as the immediate site of obstruction, light, responsiveness, or turning back, rather than as six architectural doors. The phrase occurs 116 times in 84 allowlisted texts. Zhongfeng says, "there is a phrase at the staff-head, beneath the straw sandals, three thousand miles away, and at the gates of the six faculties; if recognized at the gates of the six faculties, there is no need to seek separately three thousand miles away" (有一句子在六根門頭，向六根門頭薦得). Yuanwu describes the six faculty-gates as "clean-naked and bare" and then says the audience will not "turn the light around and look back" (六根門頭淨裸裸赤灑灑，只是不肯回光返照). Huangbo's record speaks of scraping and clearing at the gates of the six faculties until not a hair of greed or craving remains untreated (於六根門頭刮削併當，貪愛有纖毫治不去). Later addresses say a "natural ancient buddha" constantly "shines light and shakes the earth at the gates of the six faculties" (六根門頭放光動地), while Ying'an describes them simply as "bare" throughout the twelve double-hours. These are observable predicates and locations assigned by the texts; the entry does not substitute a general theory of sensation.

To have a discerning eye: to be able to recognize, distinguish, or judge what an encounter puts forward. Danxia Tianran asks whether the person who fed a traveler has such an eye, and Muzhou Daoming asks the same about a donor after an unnamed participant returns from a meal. Fayan Wenyi explicitly tells an unnamed participant that his earlier question shows a discerning eye, then asks why he did not cover the exchange before the public assembly. Jiashan Shanhui gives the negative boundary: someone who depends on buddha-and-patriarch sayings as a model has not yet acquired the eye. Fayun Faxiu promises the eye if listeners can identify the color of the wind. Yuanwu Keqin asks those with the eye to judge whether Xuedou or the Buddha has exposed the other. Tiantong Hongzhi says an eye-equipped Chan participant will recognize and assent to his sequence of circle figures; Sanshan Lai says such a discerning guide departs as soon as the matter is raised. Mingjue Cong uses the forehead-eye expansion when he says the teaching seat should make each person discerning and impartial underfoot. Chan bends ordinary possession of sight into a public capacity that named speakers confer, question, demand, and test; it is not a physical-eye diagnosis and not automatic approval of every claim.

The base form, the qualified correct-eye form, and the forehead-eye form belong to one discernment family here; the longer forms specify qualification or location but do not name different faculties. Nominal English ('one with a discerning eye') and verbal English ('to have a discerning eye') are grammatical renderings of the same property, not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: To be complete, fully endowed, or lacking nothing. Xuansha says, “each person is fully endowed; each person is manifest” (人人具足，人人成現). Another address ranges across monastics and laypeople, women and men, wise and foolish, noble and low, saying all are fully endowed “without the least lacking” (悉皆具足，曾無欠少). Hongzhi pairs “fully endowed from the beginning” (本來具足) with “not a hair's breadth lacking, not a hair's breadth in excess.” A later text warns that merely accepting “fully endowed from the beginning, no need to seek outside” can become empty talk. In the ordination compound “full precepts” (具足戒), the same completeness word modifies the precepts: biographies record receiving or being given the full precepts. Predicate and attributive placement express the same completeness, not different lexical referents.

Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, arrival within integration (兼中到) is the fifth named relation. Dongshan’s verse places it outside the opposition of existence and nonexistence; later records repeatedly describe distinctions as exhausted or integrated. Dongshan Liangjie begins the fifth-rank verse by saying it falls into neither existence nor nonexistence. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives it a dawn verse, while an unnamed monastic asks Fenyang Shanzhao for it and receives images of a weaving jade woman and a drumming stone man. Langting Ting uses a returning cuckoo, Juelang Daosheng offers a later black-white diagram, Yongjue Yuanxian says affairs and principle are both gone, and Ruibai Mingxue applies it to a shout after holy and ordinary, subject and object, and existence and nonexistence are exhausted. These remain attributed illustrations of one rank.

SearchAliases: know hot and cold for oneself
Senses.Explanation: Knowing hot and cold for oneself is the recurrent predicate of the drinking-water comparison: the person concerned, not another reporter, knows the temperature. Literally, one knows cold and warmth for oneself, usually in the comparison “like a person drinking water, knowing hot and cold for himself” . Huiming uses it after Huineng's instruction to report that he now has an entry; Huangbo joins it to conduct in each movement, dwelling, and instant; and other teachers pair it with looking for oneself rather than seeking from another. The phrase also becomes an object of interrogation: Longmen Foyan grants that hot and cold can be known, then asks what the one who knows for himself is. Daodu pairs “knowing hot and cold for oneself” with “handling slow and urgent matters for oneself” and says the matter cannot be spoken out even when both parties exert themselves. The Chan bend is this sensory commonplace's use as a first-person report, an answer about the Way, and a question about the knower; the texts preserve the water comparison and these recorded deployments.

Senses.Explanation: Its recorded neighbors make the image concrete: “the cold furnace has no smoke; a bean pops in cold ashes” (寒爐煙絕，冷灰豆爆); a public question asks, “leaving aside a withered tree flowering, what about when a bean pops in cold ashes?” and receives “a thunderclap on level ground” (平地一聲雷). Other addresses follow the phrase with impossible growth—stone bamboo shoots sprout, flame comes from an icy river, an iron tree flowers, and a wooden man claps—or simply with “suddenly, one sound” (驀地一聲). The corpus also speaks of “a person in whom a bean has popped in cold ashes” (冷灰豆爆底人), making the image an appraisal in an interview. Zen bends a domestic image of an unlikely pop from spent ash into a stock address and interview phrase, repeatedly paired with sound and impossible renewal. Those pairings are the texts’ own; this entry assigns no hidden event to the image.

Senses.Explanation: The paired phrase names ordinary feelings and holy views together as a two-sided obstruction or contrast. Caoshan Benji calls them the “golden lock on the dark road” and says one must mutually interchange (凡情聖見是金銷玄路，直須回互). Sanfeng Hanyue Fazang says there is no need to remove the pair before cold fills the whole sky and heat fills it. Chaozong Tongren calls ordinary feelings and holy views the road of birth and death, then contrasts exhausting the feelings of holy and ordinary with the road out of birth and death, while warning that this remains reciprocal treatment. Yongjue Yuanxian repeats the golden-lock formula and says earlier sages used the teaching to winnow it away. These deployments treat both poles as a coupled conceptual formation, not as praise of the holy half.

Senses.Explanation: An emphatic warning governing an action or error: literally 'urgently avoid,' hence 'strictly avoid,' 'take care not to,' or 'beware of.' The object supplied by the record must be translated rather than replaced by a general spiritual warning. Daowu says, 'where knowledge does not reach, strictly avoid speaking of it' (智不到處，切忌道著); Daoqian answers a question about words that display the Way with 'strictly avoid choosing' (切忌揀擇); Tianyin tells the assembly 'strictly avoid conjecturing' (切忌卜度). Other high-seat warnings preserve concrete allusions: 'the sword has long gone; strictly avoid marking the boat' (劍去久矣，切忌刻舟), and 'if you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, beware being branded on the forehead' (不是龍門客，切忌遭點額). Its Chan deployment is a direct warning embedded in interviews and public addresses, not a commentator's private aside.
