Senses.Explanation: The phrase names movement or conduct “among different kinds,” and Chan records make it a contested classification of how a person goes rather than a zoological destination. Nanquan Puyuan says that Chan monks “must move among different kinds” (須向異類中行), answers Guizong Zhichang’s animal-conduct objection, and elsewhere classifies Daowu Yuanzhi’s withdrawal from an exchange as “moving among different kinds” (他却是異類中行). Caoshan Benji repeats Nanquan’s classification while discussing forms of speech. Langting Ting distinguishes moving among different kinds without cutting off sound and form as the “following fall” (隨墮), alongside the kind-fall and honored-fall. Xieyun Ji uses the phrase of a cat in a playful letter, while Juelang Daosheng tells Huang that earlier people required moving among different kinds and contrasts this with being soaked dead in still water. The shared wording therefore covers named conduct, classification, question-and-answer, and later explanation; the records do not reduce these deployments to a single animal act.

Senses.Explanation: To draw a snake and add feet is to spoil a sufficient figure by adding what does not belong. Langting Jingting applies the phrase to describing an incomparable mind with an added moon image. Huanglong Huinan uses it for saying more than one's share requires; Shanfeng Xian calls his own further remark an added foot; Juelang Daosheng says the ancestral style never needed such additions. Yuan'an Feng playfully reverses the result—adding feet makes a dragon—while Danxia Dangui tags an old question as the needless addition. The shared Chan test is whether extra speech clarifies the live matter or merely decorates and distorts it.

SearchAliases: a painted cake cannot satisfy hunger
Senses.Explanation: A painted cake is repeatedly named as something that cannot feed: the records apply that bodily limit to words, talk, blows, and shouts that likewise fail to satisfy hunger. Literally a cake drawn or painted rather than edible. Chan records make it a stock verdict by completing the image: “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” . In the Xiangyan case, after he cannot answer Guishan's question and searches all the writings he has read for a reply, he sighs, “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” ; the record then has him burn those writings. Dahui's verse pairs it with another ineffective likeness: “how could a shimmering mirage ever stop thirst? When could a painted cake fill hunger?” . The verdict extends beyond writings. One discourse says “discussing the obscure and speaking of the marvelous is like using a painted cake to fill hunger” ; another asks whether wielding the staff and shouting differs from filling hunger with a painted cake . A verse explicitly places it beside “speaking of food never makes one full” . Thus the object keeps its literal non-feeding property while the corpus repeatedly applies it to quoted words, explanations, stock gestures, and other substitutes that it says do not fill hunger.

Senses.Explanation: at the very place concerned. Chan records repeatedly couple it with results said to occur without going elsewhere: liberation 'right where it is,' arising right there and appearing wherever one goes, quiescence right there, and the place of teaching right there. In public exchanges it also retains its direct locative force: when a visitor quotes 'without leaving the very place, constantly clear,' the identified master is asked where that is. Another discourse asks how one recognizes the buddhas and immediately surpasses them right there. These predicates and questions load an ordinary locative expression within Chan discourse.

to miss what is directly before one
Senses.Explanation: To miss something face-to-face is to fail to recognize what is directly present; speakers apply the warning to a person, ordinary sights, a staff, and an encounter before the assembly. The phrase occurs as a verdict, a warning, and an author's acknowledgment. Meixi Du pairs two kinds of people: those who stand out shoulder it directly, while those confused about the head and recognizing a shadow miss it face-to-face (超群拔萃的，直下荷擔；迷頭認影的，當面錯過). In a letter he says that on first meeting a correspondent he did not recognize the correspondent's freedom and literary quality, “truly what is called missing it face-to-face” (誠所謂當面錯過也); this is the corpus's only formula using “what is called” for the term. Boshan Wuyi says, after asking whether anyone can assess the value of what he has presented, “one still must not miss it face-to-face” (也不可當面錯過). Elsewhere Boshan lists “rice comes from grain, soup from water, and a nun is a woman,” then says “do not miss it face-to-face” (飯是米做底、湯是水做底、師姑是女人做底，切莫當面錯過). Yunxi's record places the warning after “kites fly and fish leap; mountains stand and water flows” (鳶飛魚躍，山峙水流，切莫當面錯過). Panlong calls on his staff to bring news to the assembly, warns them not to miss it face-to-face, raises the staff, and asks whether they understand. The exact phrase occurs 134 times in 67 allowlisted files.

Senses.Explanation: A mass of doubt is something cultivated until it becomes concentrated and then breaks open or is shattered at awakening. The Chan record makes doubt materially mass-like: a discourse says that inside and outside ‘roll into one mass of doubt’ (滾作一箇疑團), and other records speak of making the whole body, sitting, walking, dressing, eating, and even the encountered world into that mass. The same physical grammar governs its end: it is ‘broken through’ (打破疑團), or remains ‘unbroken’ (疑團不破). In an autobiographical public account, repeated blows make Gaofeng Yuanmiao's mass of doubt more acute (疑團愈切). Thus the phrase is not merely ordinary uncertainty; these later Chan records deploy it as the consolidated, bodily condition named around sustained investigation and its reported breaking. The corpus does not make the mass a separate object from the doubt or state a further gloss for the breaking.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names a sustained, felt condition of doubt used in inquiry, not a passing uncertainty about a proposition. Wuyi Yuanlai explicitly asks what this doubt is and describes it erupting, knotting at the brows, and becoming impossible to put down or drive off. Dahui Zonggao says that while it remains unbroken, life and death press in. Gaofeng Yuanmiao recounts it suddenly arising while he held the question where the one returns, leaving him unable to distinguish directions. Librarian Lai tells Xueyan Zuqin that investigating Chan requires raising it and connects small doubt with small awakening. Preface author Ding Libiao calls not knowing a parent's destination or one's own beginning and end the great doubt of life and death shared across time. Zhongfeng Mingben warns that even uninterrupted conjunction of saying and doubt can become a subtle stealing mind. The corpus thus presents a concentrated condition to be raised and broken, while also warning against treating its continuity as achievement.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 1,103 hits in 235 files and 230 works. Seven witnesses across six independent works meet the packet floor and cover definition, bodily description, unbroken condition, autobiography, instruction, preface formulation, and critique.

Senses.Explanation: To make something clear or bring it to light. Chan biographies repeatedly say that someone brings “the great matter,” “the mind-ground,” or “the essentials of mind” to light. One record lists bringing the great matter to light alongside having one's mind-ground opened through mountains and waters and recognizing one's original face through things encountered; the text supplies these neighboring predicates without making them synonyms. A later address states its aim as having each person “directly bring to light one's own fundamental great matter” (直下發明自己本分大事), anchoring direct instruction rather than retrospective biography. Other biographies say “there will certainly be clarification” (必有發明) or that someone was “not greatly clarified” (不大發明). Those result and degree constructions name the outcome of the same bringing-to-light event, not another lexical referent.

Senses.Explanation: To swear an oath is to make an explicit pledge; the surviving witnesses record different oath contents and do not all describe a public performance. The Xuefeng Genxin row is compiler biography: it says he vowed to travel and then went to Gushan, not that he utters the headword. Another biography records a private vow to travel to China, a training text says one must vow in order to endure discipline, and Baozhi recalls a vow made with an Indian monk. The common element is an explicit pledge, while publicity is not established as defining.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make the top of a hundred-foot pole the place where gaining entry is still insufficient and a further step is demanded, questioned, or refused. Changsha Jingcen’s verse says that even one who has gained entry is not yet genuine and must step forward from the pole-top, with the ten directions as the whole body. Wumen transmits Shishuang’s question asking how to advance, and Fojian Huiqin comments on the moment of advancement. An unnamed monastic puts the fixed question to Fadeng, while Yanguan Qi’an counters by asking what use advancement would have. These divergent responses preserve the pole-top as a public challenge rather than a fixed ladder stage.

Senses.Note: The literal anatomy and the idiomatic qualification do not require separate senses here: the records explicitly connect blood under skin to knowing pain and itch, preserving the bodily predicate inside the transferred use. “A person who can feel pain” is therefore an alternate contextual rendering, not an interpretive second sense.

SearchAliases: to have blood under the skin
a person who can feel pain
Zen have blood under the skin
Senses.Explanation: Blood under the skin is the records' bodily image for someone who registers pain and itching, unlike unresponsive earth and wood. It is consequently used by Gulin Qingmao as a qualification for people addressed in the hall: "you people must have blood under the skin" (汝諸人須是皮下有血始得), and "if he has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood" (他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯). A garden exchange also keeps the literal body image audible: seeing a cook cut melons, Yu'an Zhiji asks the head cook, "which one has blood under the skin?" (那個皮下有血). Zen bends the bodily phrase into a recurrent test for someone who registers a touch or blow, while the records themselves ground that use in pain and itching rather than an imported psychological category.

Senses.Explanation: The whole earth names the maximal terrestrial field brought under a statement. Speakers use it in comparisons, declarations, and encounter formulas: the whole earth may be gathered, called a gate, treated as a person's eye, or included in an appraisal. The phrase supplies the scope of those claims; it does not by itself explain or endorse them.

The two Yuanwu witnesses repeat a related formula and are not needed to manufacture independence: Xuefeng, Shangfeng Huihe, Yinyuan Longqi, Yulin Tongxiu, and Yuanwu deployments already preserve cross-work spread. Senses.Explanation: The monastery supervisor is the administrator who records, allocates, and safeguards communal property and practical business. A dying elder orders the supervisor to record the division of robes and bowls; public records thank incoming and outgoing supervisors, and named officeholders request formal addresses or receive verses and memorial rites. The office belongs to the monastery's administrative side: being 監寺 does not by itself make its holder the presiding teacher.

Senses.Explanation: People described as unable to see, hear, and speak. In the Chan record, the full phrase becomes the stable wording of Xuansha Shibei's “three kinds of invalids” public case. Xuansha asks how one receives people who cannot see a raised mallet or whisk, hear spoken command, or answer. Yuanwu Keqin warns his audience against treating his discussion as nothing more than the disability list, then asks where the blind, deaf, and mute fellow stands; Xuedou Chongxian begins his verse with the same phrase. In a Yunmen case, Yunmen tests an unnamed monk for deafness and muteness, and Xuedou applies the full phrase to him. Yuelin Shiguan later labels and re-asks Xuansha's case. Guting Shanjian also compares people unable to resolve doubt with the blind, deaf, and mute. Zen bends a literal description into repeatable wording for a public case and an interview about receiving people when visible, audible, and spoken exchange fails; the entry does not invent a diagnosis beyond each recorded deployment.

Senses.Explanation: The records define straight mind against bends, twists, crookedness, and falseness: ‘straight mind means without bends or twists.’ Literally, a straight or straightforward mind. The term occurs 163 times in 89 allowed texts. The corpus supplies two compact definitions: 'straight mind means without bends or twists' (直心者，無委曲故), and 'straight mind is the site of the Way because it has no falseness' (直心是道場，無虛假故). The Platform Record repeats 'straight mind is the site; straight mind is the clean land' (直心是道場，直心是淨土), then contrasts inwardly acting crookedly while verbally speaking straight with actually carrying out straight mind. Its positive clause is 'only carry out straight mind; regarding all things, have no grasping' (但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著). Another address expands the pattern into four coordinated expressions: 'straight mind is the site; straight speech is the subtle teaching; straight conduct is subtle conduct; straight verification is the subtle result' (直心是道場，直說是妙法，直行是妙行，直證是妙果). The common collocation 'straight mind and straight conduct' (直心直行) occurs 24 times in 17 texts. One record describes it by the absence of self-versus-other, right-versus-wrong, falseness, and crookedness; another uses 'straight mind, straight conduct, original color, original share' (直心直行，本色本分) to characterize a named Chan figure's meetings with people.
Senses.Note: The English follows the graph meaning 'straight' (直) and the texts' own oppositions: straight versus crooked (直／曲), genuine versus false (genuine / false), and straight conduct versus flattering crookedness (諂曲). The direct definition 'without bends or twists' occurs once, while the site-of-the-Way formula occurs across multiple independent records. No master-specific sense is warranted.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make this action a lineage banner for Bodhidharma’s coming while also turning it into a question and a claim that teachers qualify in their own words. Dahui Zonggao twice states the Bodhidharma formula and glosses direct pointing as what every person already has. Huitang Zuxin and Yuanwu Keqin place it in lineage discourse, while Yuanwu also says the branching lineage has no destination outside it. An unnamed monastic asks Juelang Daosheng what the paired formula means. Mengan Siyue compares it to an antelope hanging by its horns, resisting a flat explanatory capture. The evidence supports the recurring banner and its public testing without treating Bodhidharma as the grammatical speaker whenever he is named.

Senses.Explanation: For two parties to deceive or lead each other astray. Frozen-corpus concordance: 207 exact hits in 111 storage files representing 109 independent works. Chan records repeatedly place this ordinary reciprocal act under negation in the assurance, ‘Only provide the assenting heart; we certainly will not deceive one another’ (但辦肯心。必不相賺), with graphic variants in the verb ‘provide’ and the adverb ‘certainly.’ Yuanwu Keqin closes an address with that formula. Dahui Zonggao uses it after answering an interlocutor's request about how to receive and keep a statement. Zhongfeng Mingben quotes the old formula and elsewhere tells a Chan student to trust his words because they will not deceive one another. Puan Yinsu repeats the assurance, but also asks whether an old worthy's saying amounts to mutual deception (古人恁麼道。莫是相賺麼). Affirmative, negative, and interrogative forms retain the same reciprocal act; the Zen-specific bend is the formula's recurring use as a public assurance tied to an assenting heart.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes one's eyebrows fall out in these Chan records. Its wording is the eyebrows (眉毛) fall out (墮落). Frozen-corpus concordance: 7 exact hits in 6 storage files representing 6 independent works. The wider family includes "the eyebrows fall" (眉毛落, 48 occurrences), "are the eyebrows still there?" (眉毛在麼, 79), and "the eyebrows become tangled together" (眉毛廝結, 129). Chan records use the loss of eyebrows as a stated consequence or accusation attached to handling Buddhist or Chan speech: one comment says that making a Buddhist teaching-discussion of a line "implicates Shimen, whose eyebrows fall out" (若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落); another points to "the place where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out" while reviewing the Cuiyan exchange. A question joins the phrase to Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha and asks why the monastery director's eyebrows fall out. The exact phrase is late and sparse, but its eyebrow-loss family is widely transmitted; the texts do not provide an anatomical explanation, and this entry adds none.

Its wording is ‘look at the talk’: look at the word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out in a record. The compound most often occurs in ‘look at the saying's head’ (看話頭), and the local wording—not an imported technical label—determines whether English says word, saying, question, or thread. The records include the recorded questioner seeking written direction because the saying he was looking at had not opened to him. They also preserve criticism: Mingben reports people calling looking at a saying ‘doing work’ and rejects their appeal to direct transmission; Yuancheng says an old hunter neither did work nor looked at a saying before answering that there was ‘no place to set a hand,’ and contrasts this with looking left and right at one's own selected saying. Another record demands, ‘if you recognize it and can say it, come out and say it—what does the end of the talk say?’ Thus the Zen deviation is an ordinary act of looking directed at actual words in recorded exchanges and itself subjected to criticism in the record.

Senses.Explanation: Sand getting into the eye is the stock image of something the eye cannot admit. The Chan record preserves Baishui Benren’s paired saying that the eye cannot take sand and the ear cannot take water, then sets it against the contrary image of an eye containing Mount Sumeru. Baishui Benren states the pair and answers a request for its meaning with “a worthy one without peer.” Hongzhi Zhengjue later quotes the complete exchange. Shending Yikui places “the eye cannot take sand” opposite “the eye contains Mount Sumeru,” making the incompatible capacities explicit in one address. Chushi Fanqi repeats both the exclusion and inclusion formulas and assigns them to contrasting ways of coming and going. Linye Qi invokes the sand-and-water pair after saying that even a displayed auspicious scene would still incur a beating. Daowu Wujin Wen turns the image transitively: if the assembly cannot name the incense burner’s color, he has put sand in their eyes and water in their ears.

Senses.Explanation: The many blind people feeling an elephant each encounter a part and mistake partial contact for the whole animal. Xiangtian Jinian explicitly reads the elephant comparison as exposing the illness of clinging to one's own view. Dahui Zonggao lists it among cases that must be met personally rather than settled in speech. Xutang Zhiyu says the blind know an elephant yet do not see the whole; an unnamed questioner asks Zhaozhou what the true elephant is when each gives a different account, and Zhaozhou answers that there is no reliance—one simply does not know. The Chan bend turns the comparison into a public test of whether partial descriptions are being promoted as complete seeing.

Senses.Explanation: To deceive people is a recurring adverse judgement on words, conduct, or inherited interpretations. The phrase retains that ordinary act while Chan records put it under public pressure. Yunmen asks for a saying that does not deceive people, then supplies the substitute response, “Do not say this is the one that deceives people.” Miyun Yuanwu states that deceiving people is no good affair and that a good affair does not deceive people; Fushi Tongxian publicly raises the positive half. Shiyu Mingfang attacks people who deceive others for gain, while Wuzhun Shifan distinguishes deceiving people from deceiving oneself. In the Blue Cliff Record, Longya Judun denies that patriarchs and buddhas intend deception but says that, because people cannot pass through, they nevertheless become deceivers. The phrase therefore becomes a test of sayings, speakers, hearers, and self-deception without losing its transitive meaning or allowing the entry to infer intent where Longya denies it.

Senses.Explanation: Intellectual understanding is knowing reached through interpreting or explanation. The corpus overwhelmingly uses the term as a rebuke or warning. Its flagship form is 'a follower of the intellectual-understanding lineage' (知解宗徒, 35 occurrences), a label applied to Shenhui and Guifeng Zongmi: even Shenhui and Guifeng were rejected as followers of intellectual understanding (神會、圭峰尚斥為知解宗徒). In an origin case, a student names the matter 'Buddha-nature at the original source,' and Huineng says that even if this fellow later founds a place, he will become only a follower of intellectual understanding (此子已後設有把茅蓋頭，只成得箇知解宗徒). Another passage puts a whole list of teaching styles under the same verdict (此等見解盡屬知解宗徒). The common gate-entry warning 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) occurs 80 times. Mi'an Xianjie continues by comparing its non-arising to the king's sword. Other records say people are deceived by intellectual understanding and conjecture (多被知解卜度瞞過), or that the matter is not an affair on the side of intellectual understanding (不是知解邊事). The headword occurs 1,186 times in 237 allowlist texts. This entry reports the corpus's repeated pejorative deployment without turning it into a general theory of mind. Huangbo Xiyun extends the term through a food-and-digestion comparison: 'what is called intellectual understanding not digested is all poison' (所謂知解不消。皆為毒藥). Parallel witnesses preserve the same wording in two other collections.
Senses.Note: A corpus-wide pejorative. The origin rebuke and the naming of Shenhui and Zongmi as followers of intellectual understanding (知解宗徒) are raised material, while 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) is a stock proclamation. Compare distinguishing, deliberation, emotional consciousness, and conjecture without treating them as automatic synonyms.

Senses.Explanation: The stone woman is an impossible animated figure who bears a child, dances, sings, plays music, or acts beside a wooden man in recurrent verses and answers. The stone woman is a stock impossible mother and actor in Chan verse, answers, and formal addresses. The record repeatedly makes her bear a child, says she has no husband, or pairs her with the wooden figure while she sings, dances, nods, plays a reed organ, or calls back a dream. Pumen Xibian groups 'the stone woman bears a child' with dust rising from a well bottom, waves rising on a mountaintop, and an empty flower bearing fruit. Dongshan Liangjie pairs the wooden figure singing with the stone woman dancing. Qingshan Shoulong answers an auspicious-sign question with the wooden figure clapping a board in the clouds and the stone woman playing a reed organ beneath the water. Hongzhi Zhengjue answers a question about the person who neither comes nor goes by saying that the stone woman calls back the three-realm dream while the wooden figure cuts off the workings of the six gates. Baiyu Si compares being forced to speak with forcing the stone woman to bear a child and making a rooster lay an egg. Yandang Wenji likewise answers a lineage question with a barren woman bearing a child. Shu'an Fancong's verse says the stone woman has no husband. These reproductive and impossible-action predicates concern one stock woman; the research found no separate stone statue or named person.

Senses.Explanation: Polishing a tile to make a mirror names the task Nanyue declares impossible in his exchange with Mazu, and later records reuse it as a comparison for wasted effort. The impossible task of polishing a tile into a mirror. In the defining encounter Nanyue Huairang polishes a tile and tells Mazu Daoyi that he is making a mirror; when Mazu objects, Huairang asks how sitting Chan could then make a buddha . Later masters use the compact expression as the case-name and bend the impossible craft in several directions. Fachang Yiyu compares private explanations and forced elaboration to polishing a tile to make a mirror . Shending Yikui groups it with striking the cart or ox and calls both children's play . Tian'an Sheng includes it in a rapid list of ancestral demonstrations judged excessively solicitous . Luyan He first compares sitting Chan to making a meal from steamed sand, then says polishing a tile to make a mirror is using a straight hook to angle for a fierce dragon . Thus the records do not only label futile effort: they preserve Huairang's public correction and repeatedly reopen its impossible action in later teaching.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the meaning of the patriarch's coming from the West
AlternateTargets: the point of Bodhidharma's journey from the West
Senses.Explanation: The meaning or point of the patriarch's coming from the West, with the patriarch understood in these records as Bodhidharma coming to China. The words usually form a stock public question rather than a request for travel history. Named respondents answer with a cypress, washing feet, a Chan board, ripe plums, a fan, landscape lines, a refusal, or a demand that the questioner turn toward his own intent. Dahui Zonggao can also name it as a topic for which there is not yet time to speak, and Zhongfeng Mingben warns that interchangeable verbal explanations miss it. The phrase therefore names one recurring question whose Chan force lies in the publicly testable answer, not a fixed route or a single explanatory paraphrase.
Senses.Note: Frozen-corpus concordance: 2,387 exact apparatus-clean hits in 279 files and 274 independent works in the canonical f001 preflight. The bare phrase and the full question belong to one referent; response diversity does not create separate senses because every response is presented as answering or discussing the same question.

Senses.Explanation: A Chan monastery is the named residential institution in which an abbot presides and a recorded teaching career is located. Lamp colophons identify Puming and Huirì Yunwen through the Chan monasteries where they serve as abbots. Transmission rosters attach named lineage figures to Baoing Chan Monastery, while collected-record contents organize successive bodies of sayings by Ciyun, Lianfeng, and Shousheng Chan Monasteries. A preface treats restoring Zhaojue Chan Monastery from overgrown ground as a major institutional act. The Chan bend is documentary and public: the monastery is not generic scenery but the named seat that locates a lineage figure, an abbacy, a body of sayings, and the restoration or transmission of the lineage.

Senses.Explanation: The Mirror of Qin is a named mirror repeatedly brought into Chan verse and exchange as an instrument before which a form, a speaking participant, or the person himself is exposed and distinguished. In the Recorded Sayings of Master Baiyu, Baiyu Jingsi says that before the mirror a jackal has no way to hide its original form; in the Recorded Sayings of Konggu Daocheng, Konggu Daocheng hangs the mirror at the head of a staff and says that every dust-mote land becomes responsive. In direct questioning recorded in the Recorded Sayings of Master Hansong, Hansong Zhicao answers after the absence of the mirror prompts the question how one can distinguish the matter. The compilers Jing and Yun, narrating Xuefeng Yicun's biography in the Zutang Collection, place Xuefeng face-to-face with the mirror and tell him to inspect himself. These are observable deployments of the mirror in appraisal and exposure, not a claim that every mention carries one secret fixed meaning. The headword occurs 29 times in 25 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: A flower in empty space is an apparent flower where no external flower stands. The stored Chan witnesses call the three realms flowers in empty space, pair true speech and false speech with flowers in empty space and the moon in water, say dream-illusion flowers need not be grasped, and compare seeing and hearing to flowers in empty space. These uses consistently present an appearance or image as lacking the solid object a viewer might seize, but the present evidence does not store the diseased-eye formula that would explain its optical cause.

Senses.Explanation: a nest or mortar; in the Chan record, a fixed mould into which words and conduct settle. The corpus speaks of falling into another's rut (墮他窠臼, "fall into his fixed rut") as oil enters flour and cannot get out, and of both inherited gestures and current fashions as ruts: "killing buddhas and patriarchs" falls within the old people's enclosure, while wielding the staff and shout does not escape the present-day rut (殺佛殺祖，盡落古人圜繢；行棒行喝，不脫今時窠臼). One record pairs new and old while saying "jump out of the rut" (一新一舊，跳出窠臼). The decisive corpus warning is recursive: pupils may mistake the identified master's refusal to establish a rut and thereby make "no rut" into a rut (以無窠臼為窠臼, "take having no rut as a rut"). Thus the Chan deviation is not merely an ordinary habit: the term names repeatable religious speech, gestures, formats, and even anti-formulas once followers preserve them as a template.

Senses.Explanation: One instruction says that in traveling on foot and dwelling in the world one must first “establish firm footing, not be stirred by the eight winds” (立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓). A verse places it as a rock amid vast waves; a public exchange receives the direct interjection, “establish firm footing well” (立定腳跟好). The corpus also corrects a rigid use of the phrase: Zhean Jingfan says that always establishing firm footing can, upon close examination, be “a one-sided, withered understanding and a dull fellow who does not comprehend adaptation” (偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢). Zen therefore bends bodily footing into a recurrent instruction and appraisal for remaining steady, while preserving a recorded warning that immobility itself can be faulted.

Senses.Note: One independent allowlisted source in the researched concordance clearly anchors this physical referent, so the sense remains provisional. It is placed second because the Zen-loaded figurative sense is primary in this corpus.

Senses.Explanation: The same four graphs also describe a literal bodily stance. Wuyi Yuanlai compares possessing the eye of inquiry to a skilled archer who “plants his heels firmly, then takes up the bow and sets the arrow, and only then can hit the target” (立定腳跟，然後拈弓架箭，始能中的). Here the phrase names what the archer physically does before shooting, not a second reading of figurative steadiness.

Senses.Explanation: “Where you stand is all genuine” is paired with acting as host wherever one is, then repeated as a Fayan-house characterization and as a predicate of immediate use. Literally, at the place of standing or taking one's position , all is genuine or real : "where you stand is all genuine." It occurs 35 times in 24 allowlisted texts. Linji's record supplies the governing formula twice: "act as host wherever you are; where you stand is all genuine; arriving circumstances cannot turn you around" . The second passage precedes it with "do not receive another person's delusion" and follows it by warning that a single doubtful thought gives an opening. Jingtu Huimin reverses its paired order as "where you stand is all genuine; act as host according to the place" . Zhongyan Huayan Zujue attaches it to "take it up and immediately use it" , while Zhenjing Kewen explicitly quotes Linji's wording as "bring it and immediately use it; where you stand is all genuine" . Chan bends the ordinary idea of a standing-place into a stable Linji roster phrase about taking the host position amid changing circumstances; the entry reports the formula and its transmitted predicates without adding a claim beyond those recorded predicates.

Senses.Explanation: To raise or hold upright the whisk, the teaching-seat implement and emblem of authority. The action occurs as an answer, demonstration, and object of public questioning rather than as a gesture with one fixed message. Nanta Guangyong answers a question about Manjusri's teacher by raising the whisk. Zhaozhou Congshen raises it when asked whether he will receive the person who sets the realm in order. Yuanwu Keqin twice raises it and says, "Just this is it." Yunmen Wenyan reopens an older exchange in which a monk asks Zifu Zhensui the import of the ancients picking up the mallet and raising the whisk. Deshan Yuanming classifies raising a finger and raising the whisk as a dead phrase. In the dominant spelling, Baiyu Jingsi raises the whisk and asks whether the assembly sees, while Yinyuan Longqi raises it as his answer to a new-command question and then tests the monk's shouts. The Zen bend is the action's institutional and interview setting: it is the presiding master's implement raised as an answer or challenge, while the corpus refuses a universal symbolic decoding. Xueyan Zuqin twice raises the whisk within hall addresses—once before calling unfreed affective dust blindness, and once before a moon verse. The surrounding sayings differ, but the referent remains the same public action with the teaching-seat implement.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 584 exact hits of the seeded spelling in 109 files / 105 works and 2,598 hits of the dominant spelling in 267 files / 263 works. Nine anchors cover direct answers, repeated demonstration, a raised old case, critical classification, and two governed dominant-spelling variants. The two spellings are readings of the same action, never separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: The top of a dung-sweepings heap is the refuse pile where discarded and filthy things collect. Chan masters repeatedly make it the unlikely place where a jewel, treasure, robe, shoe, or even a golden body is found, while also using the same heap for adding still more rubbish. Juelang Daosheng says the Buddha found a mud pellet on the heap and raised it before the assembly. Muting Pufu calls a display of pots, tiles, bamboo scraps, and bricks “adding more rubbish atop the dung heap.” Xuedou Chongxian places a sixteen-foot golden body on the heap before setting that proposition aside. Changling Zhuo’s verse says treasure is found there without seeking. Dongshan Liangjie compares joy after leaving holy truth undone to finding a bright pearl on the heap. Yehai Ziqing says he found a torn robe there and kept it for decades. Mi’an Xianjie uses the rubbish-adding frame after saying that even forgetting both delusion and awakening remains additional refuse.

Senses.Explanation: Dafang Xinghai's mountain verse is the corpus's direct plant action: he is too indolent to gather purple fungus beside the stream (懶去溪邊採紫芝). The plant-name circulates much more widely in the compound Purple Fungus Song. Tiantong Shanxin is publicly asked what that song is and answers by clapping; Fahua Quanju answers an independent transmission of the question by saying that it is not a Wu sound but must be Han speech (不是吳音，切湏漢語). Yongjue Yuanxian asks who will join a solitary recluse in singing it (中有幽人守貞獨，誰來同唱紫芝歌), Xisou Shaotan places groups of two and three singing it on stones under pine roots (三三兩兩松根石上唱紫芝歌), and Yuanwu Keqin asks who can sing it in the season of high mountains, autumn wind, and a single goose (誰當此時節，解唱紫芝歌). Wuwen Daocan separately invokes the Four Hoaryheads of Mount Shang and their heart of withdrawal, but his verse does not contain the headword. Zen bends the plant-name into a song asked about in public interviews and sung in mountain-retreat verse. The evidence does not make the bare word itself the title of a second thing.

Senses.Explanation: To begin the monastic restriction period is to formally open a fixed seasonal interval in which the resident community follows its established schedule and limits. Recorded-sayings collections commonly use the term as an occasion heading before an address or short evening instruction. Paired references to releasing the restriction mark the opposite boundary. The stored headings therefore attest an institutional calendar action, not an utterance by the record owner whose address follows.
Senses.Note: The frozen corpus has 2,188 exact hits in 273 files representing 270 independent works. Eight anchors from eight works show winter and summer openings, hall addresses, evening instruction, an imperial opening date, and explicit pairing with release of the restriction. Senses.Explanation: To revive after being cut off: the records use a death-and-revival image in a recurrent teaching-seat formula and in explicit criticism of that formula. Its dominant fixed formula is ‘let go at the cliff and personally assent and undertake it; revive after being cut off, and you cannot deceive anyone’ (懸崖撒手，自肯承當；絕後再甦，欺君不得). Records also place it after ‘the life-root is severed’ (命根斷), beside ‘shed skin and exchange bones’ (去皮換骨), and compare it with a cold ember flaming and a withered tree flourishing again. The identified master explicitly departs from the inherited formula: ‘the former sages all wanted to revive after being cut off; I am not like that.’ The entry reports this recurrent sequence and its criticism without deciding what state the phrase denotes.

Senses.Explanation: The term names an observable walking circuit or action, with records specifying its timing, direction, companions, and coordination with rest. Literally, to 'go along walking' or 'walk about.' The term occurs 1,022 times in 273 allowed texts and names an observable bodily action. A late biography makes the direction explicit: at night a recluse goes outside the crag to walk about, the visiting master follows, and 'each walks east and west' (隱者出巖外經行，師亦隨之，第東西各步). A Five Lamps address pairs physical condition and action: 'when well, walk about; when tired, rest' (健即經行困即歇). The same collection records Layman Feng Ji walking about the teaching hall with Foyan when a child recites a line, and records another unnamed questioner 'walking under the pines one evening' when he hears a mountain spring (一夕，松下經行，聞巖泉聲). In the collected old cases, Sudhana searches in all four directions for seven days and finds Meghashri 'walking slowly on another peak' (在別峰上徐步經行). Daily timing is also explicit: a biography says an unnamed questioner ate only after serving the assembly, while Bingseng watched him 'walk about after each meal' (每飯罷經行時). The term is frequently coordinated with sitting and lying as one of the body's recorded activities. These places, times, directions, companions, and contrasts support the plain action word.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas were searched; no stable nominal self-definition was found. Distinct deployment shapes retained are walking east-west at night, walking when well versus resting when tired, walking with another person in a hall, walking under pines, slow walking on another peak, and walking after a meal. The entry adds no special category beyond what the people in the records physically do.

Senses.Explanation: Vimalakirti is the pre-Zen householder whom Chan masters repeatedly raise in public interviews and comments. His exact name occurs 263 times in 116 allowlisted texts. Linquan Conglun directly notes that the Sanskrit Vimalakirti means 'Stainless Renown' and is also rendered Jingming (梵語維摩詰，此云無垢稱，亦云淨名). The dominant Chan deployment is his sickroom and silence: Manjusri asks him about entry into the gate of not-two, Vimalakirti remains silent, and later masters test that silence rather than merely repeat it. Yuanwu raises the exchange as a case; Dahui cites both Vimalakirti's account of illness and his silence; Weilin Daopei invokes the empty sickroom while addressing illness. Xuedou asks what Vimalakirti said, Fenyang would give Vimalakirti and Manjusri thirty blows, and Yun'e Xi calls his closing his mouth 'eating salt to stop thirst.' The Zen Vimalakirti is therefore the seated, sick, silent figure whom masters question, rebuke, praise, and reuse—not an imported life story.

Senses.Explanation: The organizing framework by which a lineage's inherited sayings and distinctions are arranged and identified. The image joins a net's main cord (綱) to an ancestral line or school (宗). Huiyan Zhizhao's preface to the Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目) places 'the key outlines of the five houses' (五宗綱要) beside 'the terms of the lineage framework' (綱宗語句), including the names and decisive details that an abbot is expected to know. Named-house compounds show the same category applied to particular lineages: Lin Xuan speaks of 'the Linji lineage framework' (臨濟綱宗), while Lin Zhifan writes of 'the Caodong lineage framework' (曹洞綱宗) being restored after confusion. Zhean Jingfan quotes Yantou Quanhuo: 'Only recognize the lineage framework; originally there is no actual thing' (但識綱宗，本無實法). Juelang Daosheng raises Yantou's other formula: 'For the great governing lineage framework, first one must recognize the phrase' (大統綱宗，先須識句). The term travels with verbs such as establish, uphold, display, grasp, and restore. Zen bends the net's main cord into the named structural vocabulary by which a teaching house recognizes, transmits, and publicly tests its inherited distinctions. Tianyin Yuanxiu says one must first reach the root and then know the lineage framework; Chaozong Tongren speaks of establishing that framework while distinguishing deviant alternatives. The added uses preserve an institutional-discursive framework rather than a new object.
Senses.Note: The exact headword occurs 796 times in 213 allowlisted storage files. Standard self-definition searches did not produce a simple equation; their zero results are preserved in WORK rather than printed as unattested Chinese evidence. The strongest structural evidence is Huiyan Zhizhao's explicit pairing of five-house key outlines with lineage-framework terms, Yantou Quanhuo's two transmitted formulas, and the named-house compounds. Linji and Caodong qualification does not change the referent, so one corpus-wide sense remains warranted.

Senses.Explanation: Close-woven, tightly knit, and allowing no gap; by extension, continuously and meticulously joined. Wuyi Yuanlai gives the clearest in-record definition: the brows knit with empty space, a needle cannot enter, water cannot wet it, and no hairbreadth gap is allowed. Dahui Zonggao critically reports respondents who stick an answer directly to a student's question and call that close-woven and free of affective dust; he also reports one-sentence answers called close-woven and not running away. An unnamed monk asks Yongjue Yuanxian for the close-woven house style and receives, "The golden needle does not permit knowing." Cizhou Fangnian appraises Zhanran Yuancheng's phrases as close-woven and not falling into beginning or end. Yuanwu Keqin uses the reduplicated form for what is continuous and close when set down. Yinyuan Longqi says a single mystery has three essentials, layered and close-woven so that no wind passes. The Zen bend is the qualitative transfer from textile closeness to public speech, house style, and lineage phrases: a saying or presentation is judged by whether any seam, temporal edge, or opening remains, while Dahui's reports preserve the possibility that this label itself is being criticized.

Kaifu Daoning applies it to seeking the subtle point through conceptual knowledge; Yuejiang Zhengyin joins it to rigidly waiting for verification. Senses.Explanation: A donkey-tethering stake is a post to which a donkey is fastened. Chan speakers call bodhi and nirvana, teaching collections, and fixed formulations donkey-tethering stakes. Boatman Decheng makes the verbal deployment explicit: “one phrase that fits the head—ten thousand aeons a donkey-tethering stake.” The stake remains the concrete tethering object; Zen bends it into a name for words or teachings at which someone stays tied.

Senses.Explanation: To be at a loss: unable to answer or know what move to make in an encounter. The records use the term for an unnamed monk after Hangzhou Wenxi remains silent, Emperor Daizong after Nanyang Huizhong remains silent, Li Ao after a master's silence, and another unnamed monk after Muzhou Daozong laughs. Miyun Yuanwu's hall officer, Later Baoshou, Censor Wang, and the still-studying Yaoshan Weiyan are likewise described as at a loss when a question or response leaves them with no answer. These cases ground the plain meaning in observable interview turns; they do not turn the word into an imported diagnosis of an unseen inner condition.

SearchAliases: an antelope hanging by its horns
Zen an antelope hanging by its horns
Senses.Explanation: An antelope hanging by its horns is a recurrent Chan image defined inside the corpus by the absence of anything a hunter can follow. One instruction says that when the antelope hangs by its horns, not only its tracks but even its scent cannot be found. The phrase is then moved into several public forms. Yunju is asked what it is like at that time and answers “six times six is thirty-six,” adding that there are no tracks. Buhui answers a question about taking the person but not the surroundings with “the antelope hangs by its horns without a trace; the mountain is naturally high and the water naturally deep.” A later instruction applies the comparison directly to a lineage teacher's speaking, saying that it has a small measure of correspondence only when it is like the horn-hanging antelope. Thus the corpus does not leave the image as animal lore: it makes the missing track and scent a question, numerical answer, position answer, verse line, and appraisal of teaching-seat speech. The exact phrase occurs 77 times in 38 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: ‘Old monk’ is both an ordinary designation for an elderly monk and the conventional first-person self-reference used by named teachers such as Baizhang Huaihai, Linji Yixuan, Zhaozhou Congshen, and Yunju Daoqi. The human role remains the same across narration, address, and self-reference; those grammatical settings do not create separate senses. Its characteristic Chan deployment is humble first-person self-reference in monastic speech, conventionally translated ‘this old monk’ and grammatically serving as ‘I’ or ‘me.’ Baizhang Huaihai recalls receiving Mazu Daoyi’s shout; Linji Yixuan says he sits securely and distinguishes the visitors who come; Zhaozhou Congshen redirects a public interview by saying, ‘this old monk is hard of hearing; ask loudly’; and Yunju Daoqi addresses the assembly at his final meeting. The same noun phrase also refers in narration to an old monk: Wuzhuo meets one, a raised case begins with an old monk carried by two disciples, and a record introduces ‘an old monk named Puhui.’ Speaker self-reference, third-person reference, and definiteness are contextual readings of the same human-role noun, not different things.

SearchAliases: a rat entering an ox horn
the rat driven into the ox horn

Senses.Explanation: A rat entering an ox horn is a narrowing image whose endpoints are stated differently in different passages. Dahui says to press inquiry until there is no further place to investigate, “like a rat entering an ox horn,” when the stealing mind suddenly ends. In a winter-solstice exchange, an unnamed monk asks how a patch-robed monk turns around when the yin forces are exhausted and one yang returns; Xutang Zhiyu answers with the phrase. Another instruction says to press forward day after day and month after month like the rat in the horn, and explicitly says that then a living road appears. The image can also be used as criticism: one record says that a declining lineage becomes narrower and narrower like the rat in the horn, while Ciming scolds an answer consisting of the phrase. These attested contrasts prevent the dictionary from turning the image into a fixed declaration of either hopeless dead end or guaranteed success. Chan makes the narrowing horn a public answer, an instruction, a rebuked reply, and an appraisal of a lineage's contraction. The exact phrase occurs 30 times in 24 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: To continue the lineage lamps is to carry Chan succession from predecessor to successor and from generation to generation. Yongjue Yuanxian defines the governing lamp image in the Extensive Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian: successive transmission is compared to a lamp because it breaks darkness and reveals things, and because its illumination can continue without end. His histories then call more than seventy generations an unbroken chain of linked lamps and describe them as linking the lamps while continuing the flame. Hanxiu Ruqian uses the phrase in memorial verses for succession after receiving his predecessor's blows and for two named lineage holders carrying the line in different regions. Zefeng Yue applies it to an ancestral portrait during a teaching-seat address. These uses concern public lineage continuity, not ordinary lamps physically fastened together.
Senses.Note: The exact headword has 104 occurrences in 28 allowed texts. Most belong to the book title treated in the second sense; the free phrase recurs with being unbroken, continuing the flame, succession, generations, ancestral portraits, and separate teaching regions. A complete concordance review found no independently attested hardware sense. A festival line about lamps and the moon reverses the graph order and therefore does not establish one.

Senses.Explanation: The book Linked-Lamp Essentials is a specific Chan compilation, not the act of continuing a lineage. In his self-preface, Huiweng Wuming says that he selected material from more than six hundred teachers, arranged encounters, questions and answers, comments on old and recent cases, and essential statements under each person's chapter, divided the work into thirty fascicles, and gave it this title. Li Yong's preface says the title was placed on the work and the blocks were carved for circulation. Yongjue Yuanxian later places Wuming's compilation among the five lamp records. A lineage biography records Wuming as its compiler, while Sichong's republication preface calls it the Linked-Lamp Record and recounts its printing history.
Senses.Note: This is a different thing from lineage succession: it is a named thirty-fascicle text with a compiler, contents, prefaces, printing blocks, circulation history, and an abbreviated record title. The full title occurs 77 times in 13 allowed texts; the shorter title occurs once. The explicit referent label in the preferred target keeps the distinction visible without relying on capitalization alone.

Senses.Explanation: The paired sensory objects of ear and eye: sound (聲) and visible form or color (色). Chan records do more than repeat the pair abstractly. Yongjia's exchange explicitly assigns them to the faculties — 'when eyes and ears meet sound and form' (眼耳緣聲色時) — and asks what is the substance of sound and form. Dahui makes the pair demonstrable during a public address: he raises the whisk and says, 'this is form,' strikes the Chan seat and says, 'this is sound' (這箇是色／這箇是聲). Another record gives ordinary audible examples: wind in pine trees, frogs, and crows are all sound, while saying that what one discriminates is sound and form. The corpus also predicates 'pass through all sound and form without obstruction' (透一切聲色，無有滯礙) and draws its own distinction between function 'together with sound and form' and 'the affairs of sound and form' (用同聲色而不是聲色之事). The Zen deviation is this repeated use as a named field of public testing and concrete demonstration; the graphs still denote what is heard and seen.

This is not the eye-and-ear field concretely demonstrated by a whisk and struck seat, so it remains a separate sense.

Senses.Explanation: The two outward signs in the fixed phrase 'without changing voice or expression' (不動聲色): voice or tone (聲) and facial look or demeanor (色). A record praises Huanglong's forty years presiding over a community as 'holding the seat of the community without changing voice or expression' (坐鎮道場，不動聲色); a public interview likewise asks whether something can be discerned 'without changing voice or expression.' This idiomatic human demeanor is a different referent from sounds and visible objects in the sensory field.

Senses.Explanation: Linji’s shout is a named Chan device, repeatedly paired or contrasted with Deshan’s staff and tested in later encounters. Device lists pair 'Linji's shout' with 'Deshan's staff,' and later sermons compare the shout to rushing thunder. The phrase is not merely a historical label: masters publicly ask what its purport is, demand that an unnamed monastic produce it, or declare that they have no use for it today. The corpus also polices the inherited emblem. In a later Fushi exchange, the presiding teacher strikes after being asked what indication lies beyond Deshan's staff and Linji's shout, then says that calling it 'staff-and-shout' sends one to hell like an arrow. Thus Zen bends an ordinary shout into a named lineage implement and object of later interview, imitation, comparison, and criticism; the entry reports only those recorded deployments.

Senses.Explanation: Able to act, come and go, or respond without constraint: free and at ease, at liberty, or freely. The word is attested 4,537 times in 388 allowlisted texts. Foyan Qingyuan closes an address by telling everyone to drink tea in the hall, free and at ease (堂中喫茶，自由自在). Yunmen Wenyan says that only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired (卷舒自在，應用無虧). The Yongzheng Emperor uses the result phrase “obtain great freedom” (獲大自在), while Zhean Jingfan says “unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time” (一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患). Dahui Zonggao says that one then enters birth and death and obtains great freedom (出生入死得大自在). Other records pair freedom in birth and death with freedom in coming and going, and explicitly test whether freedom at death matches ordinary freedom amid encountered objects. Zen bends an everyday freedom word into public tests about response, movement, birth, and death, while Baizhang Huaihai warns against casually declaring a buddha free or not free. Adjective, adverb, result noun, and the repeated form “free and at ease” remain grammatical deployments of the same condition.

Senses.Explanation: One’s own nature is the nature attributed to the person or mind itself. The records place it in public questions, explanations of what it contains, compound names such as ‘the naturally true buddha of one’s own nature,’ and claims about what does or does not depart from it. The expression occurs 2,091 times in 260 allowlisted texts. The Platform Record says that one's own nature is originally clean, contains the ten thousand things, and is not apart from them; another recension lists it as originally clean, not arising or perishing, complete in itself, unmoving, and able to produce the ten thousand things. These are the record's predicates, not an imported definition. Other Chan records use the term in questions about seeing, clarifying, or being unaware of one's own nature. Tianru Weize says that what is reluctantly named the naturally true buddha of one's own nature is also called the master of one's own house. Direct answers do not settle into a single formula: asked 'What is one's own nature?' Huanyou Zhengchuan says, 'I will not say'; asked about the naturally true buddha of one's own nature while tending a fire, another master tells the unnamed questioner to bring a bundle of firewood.

Senses.Explanation: As a figure for speech, the tongue is said to lack bones, be cut off, or be restrained from moving in public exchange. A person's capacity to speak is what Chan verdicts test, trust, disable, or demand under the image of the tongue. Yungai Jipeng and Chengtian Weijian each answer a public question by saying that the tongue has no bone. Guanghui Yuanlian says that he no longer doubts the tongues of old masters, and Shoushan Xingnian immediately asks him to state his understanding. Huangbo Xiyun predicts that Linji Yixuan will cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven. Longyuan Fa says that a demon king has cut off the Buddha's tongue and offers to redress the wrong. Huiyun Benchong Sheng orders a respondent to produce a statement without moving the tongue, then says the respondent's shout still involves lips and mouth. These are speech acts and verdicts, not reports of bodily injury, so they establish a Zen-loaded referent separate from the organ that can be bitten.

Senses.Note: Two independent bodily witnesses establish the ordinary anatomical referent. No special Zen deviation is asserted for it.

Senses.Explanation: A tongue dragging on the ground is speech made bodily excessive: the organ extends so far that it trails along the earth. Chan masters deploy the image as an answer about a saying, as Zhongfeng Mingben’s capping comment on a visitor’s words, and as a cost of choosing one side of a comparison. Wuzhun Shifan answers a question about Zhaozhou’s saying of no guest and host with “the tongue drags on the ground,” then answers the follow-up with “words fill the world.” Zhongfeng Mingben inserts the phrase after replaying a visitor’s answer “I came for the teaching.” Juelang Daosheng gives it as the answer requested before birth, then follows it with “eyebrows propping up heaven.” Mingjue Cong says that choosing Yunmen in his comparison would wrong himself until his tongue dragged on the ground.

Senses.Explanation: Straw sandals remain literal footwear while serving as the ordinary equipment and expense of traveling on foot through the Chan record. Footwear woven from grass or straw. In Chan records the sandals belong especially to going on foot between teachers: “to wear out straw sandals” and “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years” make the ordinary shoe part of the institutional life of itinerant inquiry. The object also enters named encounters: Deshan turns his back on the hall, puts on his sandals, and leaves; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head after Nanquan recounts cutting the cat. Huangbo calls “the patriarchs' dark purport” “worn-out straw sandals” and says bare feet would be better. The corpus records these concrete actions and comparisons without supplying a symbolic gloss for the sandals.

Senses.Explanation: Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. Chan records cite “Zhuang Zhou dreamed of the butterfly; he is not me; the butterfly dreamed of Zhuang Zhou; I am not him” (莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠), recount that when his wife died he drummed on a basin and sang, and list learning connected with Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the Hundred Schools. The corpus also deploys his name in the recurring sword line “Zhuang Zhou’s sword killed three thousand guests; from then on the road to Peach Spring did not go through” (莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通). A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?” and answers, “Zhuang Zhou alone is permitted to bring great peace” (三千劒客今何在？獨許莊周致太平). Another verse directly addresses him: “a message to Zhuang Zhou: stop deliberating” (寄語莊周休擬議). Thus the Zen Zhuang Zhou is the named dreamer, basin-drummer, learned figure, sword-line figure, and addressee that masters quote and redeploy. This entry does not supplement those deployments with an outside life story.

SearchAliases: Zen do not get it wrong
Senses.Explanation: An imperative: do not (莫) understand or take it (會) wrongly (錯). Its distinct Chan deployment is as warnings that named speakers attach directly to a saying or answer in public discourse. Asked the intention of the coming from the West, Anguo Hongtao answers 'it is so, but do not get it wrong.' An extended address says not to infer 'not round and not sudden' from the preceding words and not to present borrowed, similar, or calculated phrases as one's own understanding, repeating 'do not get it wrong.' Elsewhere Bao’en Huiming warns an assembly not to say that speech, silence, movement, and stillness are all buddha-affairs. The formula can also follow an unexplained seasonal statement — 'yesterday snow, today it melts' — leaving the warning itself as the only explicit appraisal. These contexts establish the public-interview function without supplying an interpretation of what the preceding words secretly mean.

Senses.Explanation: The records warn against collapsing into blank nothing, then answer that blankness itself is absent or is not blank. Literally, 'fall into emptiness,' but in these records the observable warning is against falling into a blank nothing. The term occurs 325 times in 128 allowed texts; the expanded form 'fall into blank annihilation' (落空亡) occurs 63 times in 37 texts. Dahui reports people who hear 'a teaching in which nothing is obtained' (無所得法) and become afraid that they will fall into blankness; he answers by asking whether the very one who fears falling into blankness is empty. A lamp dialogue answers the charge that Chan teachers mostly fall into blankness by saying that letters and other things arise from wisdom and that, when 'great function appears before one' (大用現前), there can be no falling into blankness. Another exchange dismantles the spatial wording itself: asked whether 'originally there is nothing' falls into blankness, the reply asks, 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立). The same collection says that people fear forgetting mind because they fear falling into blankness with nowhere to get hold, then says 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). There are 37 occurrences of 'not fall into blankness' (不落空) and 21 of the warning 'do not fall into blankness' (莫落空).
Senses.Note: The translation 'blankness' follows the records' direct corrections: 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立), and 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). The entry records the corpus's accusations, warnings, and replies.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): Tianbo Chongyuan is the exact hall speaker, saying that only by treading the ground step after step does one know the landing place and otherwise must step back and look underfoot.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase asks or states the place where something comes down, settles, or finds its point of application. Chan exchanges use that ordinary landing-place relation to press where a saying, action, or person’s understanding actually comes to rest. Chan records apply it to words, answers, cases, actions, people, and one's life: 'know where it lands' (知落處) occurs 770 times in 205 texts, while 'not know where it lands' (不知落處) occurs 172 times in 89 texts. Yuanwu says that as soon as Danxia raised it, he knew where it landed (才方舉起便知落處), and his Blue Cliff prose twice contrasts knowing and not knowing where Mazu's public case lands. Dahui asks whether the assembly knows where his teacher's words land and says that knowing it identifies the top graduate (還知師翁落處麼。若知落處便識得狀元). Changqing asks the cited participant, 'Do you understand where it lands?' (還委落處麼). A lamp record joins origin and destination: 'if you know where it arises, then you know where life lands' (若知起處。便知身命落處). Xiuyelin gives the richest explicit relation found: 'the fundamental matter is precisely where the person's own life-source lands' (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). The article therefore keeps the verbal image and reports what the texts assign a landing point; it does not replace that image with an imported abstraction.

Senses.Explanation: In Chan records, the image of intertwining vines denotes language that proliferates, entangles, or demands cutting through. Yuanwu Keqin directly joins the tangle to the need to cut off words, calls old cases vine-tangle cases, and elsewhere praises action that cuts the tangle straight off. Zhongfeng Mingben lists vine-Chan among defective labels and describes later students caught where vines spread everywhere. Qingshan Puning self-deprecatingly calls his unavoidable address tangling with the assembly. Dahui Zonggao says Wushang had already entered mud and water for the assembly and produced no little tangle. Lingyao Liang offers a vine-entangled proclamation for the community to disentangle together. The metaphor can criticize interpretive or case language, describe a named speaker's own speech, or name material deliberately presented for disentangling; it is not a flat synonym for every use of words. A literal-plant control searched plant predicates and collocations such as sprouting, spreading, branching, rooting, binding, covering the ground, and filling the ground. In the retained Chan uses these extend the same speech-and-case tangle—lineage talk sprouts, sayings branch, cases cover the ground, or words bind a participant—rather than describing cultivated or botanical vines. The selected evidence therefore supports one loaded tangle referent, not a hidden second plant article.
Senses.Note: Literal vegetation/concrete-entanglement controls were run across all 2,876 exact hits. Apparent plant grammar repeatedly governs discourse, sayings, cases, or lineage proliferation; no independently active botanical referent survived for this entry. Eight witnesses from five distinct works remain sufficient for the loaded sense.

Senses.Explanation: Empty space is the open expanse in which things can be located or compared. The term is attested 5,943 times in 279 allowlisted texts. Chan records also make that ordinary expanse measurable, containable, breakable, and fillable. Productive forms include "in empty space" (虛空中, 91 occurrences), "inside empty space" (虛空裏, 136), and "like empty space" (如虛空, 364). They also record impossible or emphatic actions: "empty space shattered" (虛空粉碎, 167), "break empty space" (打破虛空, 85), and "empty space burst apart" (虛空迸裂). Zhongfeng says of an incense offering, "empty space cannot contain it; the great earth cannot support it" (虛空包不住，大地載不起). Zhe'an Fan says that if one understands at a stated point, "empty space can be measured" (虛空可量). A memorial narrative describes one who raised his head and suddenly forgot confusion and awakening, "lucid like empty space, impossible to approach or lodge in" (如虛空玲瓏不可湊泊). The corpus also says "empty space has no inside or outside" (虛空無內外, 9), while a formal address says that the Chan lineage's defining feature "fills empty space, with nowhere to evade it" (充塞虛空，無處回避). These are literal comparisons and recorded predicates; no single further sense is imposed on all 5,943 occurrences.

Senses.Note: The corpus has 578 hits in 188 allowlisted texts; Toad Chan (蝦蟆禪) occurs 11 times in 10 texts. Five exact headword witnesses and one marked graphic-variant witness cover definition, answer, verse-like pairing, public exchange, appraisal, and ordinary animal enumeration. These deployments still denote the animal or its image; direct human epithets are separated below.

Senses.Explanation: The animal appears both in ordinary lists and in striking Chan sayings. Baima Ai answers a question about the pure teaching-body with a toad at the bottom of a well swallowing the moon (井底蝦蟆吞却月). Sanyi Mingyu pairs a monkey accustomed to climbing a tree with a toad jumping into a well (猢猻慣上樹，蝦蟆跳入井). In an exchange with Xinghua Cuyuan, Yang Yi says that a three-legged toad jumps into the sky (三脚蝦蟆跳上天), and Xinghua lets it jump as it pleases. Dongshan Xiaocong lists the variant-written toad with earthworms as creatures having holes. The animal also enters the named appraisal Toad Chan. Tian'an Sheng explicitly asks what Toad Chan is and describes a toad croaking like a drum in the rain and crying, “what suffering?” (蝦蟆遇天雨，叫喚聲如鼓……何苦？何苦？). Juelang Dasheng applies the same label in a public exchange. Zen bends the ordinary animal-name into answers, impossible animal actions, and a named Chan appraisal, while the records continue to use it for the creature itself.

Senses.Note: Three exact witnesses from three independent records establish direct naming and comparison of human respondents. The local rebukes differ, but each headword refers to the person rather than supplying a different reading of the animal scene.

Senses.Explanation: The same animal-name can denote a human target directly called or compared to a toad. When an interlocutor cannot supply another question, Yunmen Wenyan calls him “this dead toad” (這死蝦蟆). Chaozong Tongren says that he cast a hook for a giant fish but caught a toad (拋鉤釣鯤鯨，釣得箇蝦蟆); the addressee protests against being pressed from free status into servitude. Yinyuan Longqi calls another respondent a forehead-marked toad (點額蝦蟆) and then says he is drowned in dead water. The human target is a different thing from a toad in a well or rain, so these direct epithets remain a separate corpus-wide sense; the entry does not project the appraisal onto every animal occurrence.

Senses.Note: One concrete image. Petty contention, fame and gain, the Chu-and-Man allusion, and a universe on the horn tip all use the same snail horn; evaluative and scale-reversing readings do not create different referents.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (吹萬禪師語錄): A prose discussion recalls Zhuangzi's Chu and Man fighting over land and leaving corpses for ten thousand miles, asks whether it is true or illusory, and answers that Yao and Shun's yielding and Tang and Wu's conquests also occupy the waste of the snail's horn. Exact actor: Chuiwan Guangzhen.

Occurrences.Kwic: 蝸角蠅頭，過客競勞塵世；輝天鑑地，至寶秘在形山。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text (憨休禪師語錄): A hall address sets the passing traveler's worldly labor over snail-horn and fly-head matters beside a great treasure, bright across heaven and earth, hidden in the bodily mountain. Exact actor: Hanxiu Ruqian.

Senses.Explanation: A snail's horn supplies the minute ground for two recurrent corpus families. In prose and verse, people contend for “the minuteness of a snail's horn,” and profit and fame on a fly's head and snail's horn become an empty battle. A discussion explicitly recalls the Zhuangzi story of Chu and Man fighting over territory and leaving corpses for ten thousand miles, then places even the yielding of Yao and Shun and the conquests of Tang and Wu in “the waste of the snail's horn.” Chan verses also reverse the scale: one puts the universe on the tip of a snail's horn, while a hall address opposes the passing traveler's labor over fly-head and snail-horn matters to a great treasure hidden in the body. The minute object, its contest language, and the vast things placed on it are one image under different predicates. The Chan deviation lies in bringing the horn into hall speech and scale-reversal verse, not in assigning it a hidden meaning. The exact phrase occurs 36 times in 26 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: The minute jiaoming insect is an extremely small creature. In the Collected Guidelines of the Lineage Masters, Yuejiang Yin makes the scale explicit by saying that it builds its nest on a mosquito's eyelash, hence the descriptive alternate “mosquito-eyelash insect.” Chan verses and addresses repeatedly reverse that scale: Dahui Zonggao puts a giant turtle inside its eye; Mengshan Yi has it drain the ocean; Lia'an Qingyu is asked about its swallowing a tiger; Yinshan Can puts a night market in its eye; and Zhongfang Tianlun says it swallows five Mount Sumerus. In the Surviving Draft of the Continued Lamp, Gaofeng Yuanmiao says that such an insect has blundered into his sky-spanning net; the line occurs inside Duanya Liaoyi's biography because Gaofeng is speaking about Duanya. These are distinct large-in-small actions and comparisons involving the same tiny creature, not evidence that the headword itself means the cosmos or carries one fixed interpretation. The headword occurs 394 times in 166 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: A transmission line is the continuity that Chan records locate through cases, question-and-answer, sentences, and succession. Caoshan Benji answers the withered-tree dragon-hum question by saying that the line is unbroken. Yuanwu Keqin says that the ancients' line is unbroken because the question is in the answer and the answer in the question; elsewhere he says that differing speakers do not lose it sentence by sentence. Yunxi Langting Ting directly names precise question-and-answer as the line unbroken. Xueguan Zhiyin passes what he received onward as the continuation of Shouchang's line and the extension of Boshan's house style. Zen thus bends hereditary and bodily continuity into a documented connective line through public speech and teacher-successor transmission.
Senses.Note: Five curated anchors across independent works support this continuity sense, including teacher-successor transmission; hereditary bloodline and bodily circulation remain separate referents in the following senses.

Senses.Explanation: A hereditary bloodline is biological kinship inherited through a family. Juelang Daosheng names the father-son bloodline as inherited without interruption. Zhuanyu Guanheng calls flesh-and-blood bloodline the closest kin and asks whether that kinship could fail to respond. Father-son inheritance and flesh-and-blood relatives are different from a school's transmission line and from circulation inside a body.

Senses.PreferredTarget: monastic robe, bowl, and personal effects
Senses.Explanation: The material monastic robe, alms bowl, and, by extension, personal effects kept with them. The allowlisted corpus has 513 hits in 115 texts, including records in which the objects are thrown onto a rock, lifted, carried, guarded, inventoried, or burned with a person's other implements. Monastic regulations also name a ‘robe-and-bowl attendant’ (衣鉢侍者, 9 hits in 3 texts), who receives the seal in one installation procedure. In the Caoqi record, this attendant raises the robe associated with the object that could not be lifted at Dayu Ridge. These passages keep the material objects and their custodial office visible even where the same pair also marks succession.
Senses.Note: This first sense covers the material pair and its administrative extension to personal effects and the attendant responsible for them. It is separated from the succession-token sense because regulations can order the objects burned or placed in custody without describing succession.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the robe and bowl as evidence of lineage succession
Senses.Explanation: The same physical robe and bowl treated as passed evidence of lineage succession. The corpus records ‘transmit the robe and bowl’ (傳衣鉢, 33 hits in 28 texts), ‘entrust the robe and bowl’ (付衣鉢, 12 hits in 10 texts), and one exact occurrence of ‘robe and bowl transmitted in succession’ (衣鉢相傳). The Dayu Ridge account explicitly calls the robe ‘a token of trust.’ Yuansou Xingduan says that Huangmei's robe and bowl were entrusted to Lu, while Qining Wenyi asks which robe and bowl Lu actually transmitted. The question is recorded as a question rather than resolved here into an object different from the material robe and bowl.
Senses.Note: Historical succession does not make this sense specific to a named individual. The selected passages show the physical token, later transmission language, and a later challenge about what was transmitted. The seven required definition formulas were searched; no additional lexical self-definition was found.

Senses.Explanation: Pei Xiu (裴休) is the Tang official whom Chan records deploy as a lay questioner, patron, student of Huangbo Xiyun, and preface writer. He visits Hualin Shanjue and questions him after two tigers answer the master's call. Other records show Huangbo loudly calling 'Pei Xiu!' and questioning where he is, and later using the same name as the answer when Pei asks him to name a painted Buddha. Three lamp compilations also transmit Pei's preface on the damage caused when inherited teachings become competing doorways and weapons. Those parallel prefaces are one event, while the two added Huangbo exchanges supply distinct public uses of his name.

Senses.Explanation: To see one's own nature. Chan records place this claim in transmission formulas, instructions, questions, and explicit challenges. Hongren links it with directly becoming a buddha; a text attributed to Bodhidharma says that seeking a buddha requires it. Huangbo Xiyun answers a direct question by refusing to make nature a second object seen by a separate seeing subject. Dahui Zonggao repeats that it is required for an unerring road and immediately asks which mind recognizes and which nature is seen. Zhongfeng Mingben says direct pointing is no longer direct once it enters speech or contrivance, while Yongming Yanshou says that once nature is seen, mind and the teaching remedies both cease. The phrase names a claimed recognition, but the records repeatedly test what the grammar of a seer looking at a separate nature would wrongly add.

Senses.Explanation: Huike's fixed reply in the mind-settling case: ‘having sought the mind, I could not find it. Huike says his mind is not at ease; Bodhidharma tells him to bring the mind so it can be set at ease; Huike answers with this phrase; Bodhidharma replies that the mind has now been set at ease. Subsequent records repeatedly examine the quoted sentence. Yuanwu asks why Huike answered only this. Juelang distinguishes Huike's utterance from later students repeating the same words. Zhuanyu Heng explicitly judges Huike's reply as falling into conceptual understanding when comparing it with the flower sermon, while Wanfeng asks how the sentence should be understood and comments on it in another register. Daxiu Zhu redeploys the wording in a first-person public question and is immediately asked where he is now. Huigong Xiong presses the abbreviated grammar: if it is altogether unobtainable, what remains to regulate? These disagreements and questions concern the force of one fixed quoted reply; they do not create a second referent.
